STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Budget Estimates for the year 1966-67 as adopted by the Corporation 
of Calcutta having, in some respects, deviated from the provisions of the 
Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, it has become necessary to provide in the Act 
that in such a case the State Government may by an order give requisite 
directions to regularise the Budget Estimates so that the municipal 
administration of Calcutta may not suffer and further that so long as the 
consolidated rates and taxes determined in the Budget Estimates cannot be 
given effect to, they may be levied at the rates in force during the previous 
year. Hence this Bill. The Bill also provides that the consolidated rate on 
bustees shall not exceed 18 per cent. on the annual valuation thereof.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF POLICE, 
CALCUTTA 


ORDER 


The 2nd April 1967. 


Whereas for the prevention of riots and affrays 
and of other disturbances of the public tranquillity, 
the Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, being specially 
empowered to act under section 144 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act 5 of 1898), made 
order, dated the 29th March 1967, in respect of 
areas within the jurisdiction of Burrabazar, 
Jorasanko, Amherst Street and Muchipara police- 
Stations within the town of Calcutta; 

And whereas the apprehension of riots and affrays 
and of other disturbances of the public tranquillity 
ho longer exists ; 

Now, therefore, I, P. K. Sen, Commissioner of 
Police, Calcutta, do hereby rescind with effect from 
‘the 2nd April 1967 the aforesaid order passed under 
section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in 
respect of the aforesaid areas. 

In this order the “town of Calcutta’? means the 
area as defined in section 3 of the Calcutta Police 
Act, 1866 (Bengal Act IV of 1866). 

Given under my hand and seal this 2nd day of 
April 1967. 

P. K. SEN, 


Commissioner of Police, Calcutta.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Durgapur (Development and ٥ہدا اہ‎ of Building Operations) Act, 
1958 was enacted with the object of securing planned development of, and 
the control of building operations in, Durgapur. The Durgapur Development 
Authority constituted under the Act was, however, empowered merely to 
enforce certain directions issued by the State Government under section 4 
of the said Act. It has become now evident that besides mere enforcement 
of regulatory measures, the Authority must also undertake preparation and 
execution of development schemes necessary for securing planned develop- 
ment of Durgapur. Besides, it must have power to own a fund, to open 
bank accounts, to appoint officers and employecs, to maintain accounts, to 
‘prepare annual budget, etc. 


The present Bill seeks to remove these lacunae under the Act. Under 
the Act as proposed to be amended the Authority will have a corporate status, 
it will acquire, hold and dispose of properties, undertake preparation and 
execution of development schemes, open bank accounts, have its own fund, 
realise fees for permission to erect buildings, appoint its own officers and 
servants, etc. and will have the necessary ancillary powcrs in connection with 
them. The Authority will also have power to adopt its own budget. The 
administrative relationship between the State Government and the Authority 
has also been fully dcfined under the Act as proposed to be amended. 

JEHANGIR KABIR, 
Member-in-charge. 


CaLcurTtTa, 
The 31st March, 1967. 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM. 


Clause 6 of the amending Bill provides for creation of a Fund for the 
Durgapur Development Authority and lays down that all moneys received by 
the Authority by way of fees, charges, fines, grants, loans, etc., will be credited 
to that Fund. 

Clause 3 of the amending Bill seeks to empower the Durgapur Development 
Authority to execute Development Schemes in Durgapur Area relating to 
development of land, township, housing, water-supply, sanitation, communica~ 
tions, etc., with the approval of the State Government, and at the initial 
stage funds for these purposes will have to be provided by the Government. 

It is not possible to give any indication of the cxact financial implication 
for the State Government at this stage. When, however, the Government 
will decide to entrust any scheme to the Authority for execution and to make 
any grant or advance any loan to the Authority for the purpose, necessary 
provisions will have to be made in the budget in due course. 

JEHANGIR KABIR, 
Member-in-charge.

MODEL BY-LAWS RECULATING THE USE OF, AND PREVENTION 
OF NUISANCE IN RECARDS TO, PUBLIC WATER SUPPLY, 
BATHING AND WASHING PLACES, STREAMS, CHANNELS, 
TANKS AND WELLS 


(Under section 355 of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932.] 
Definition 


1.—~In these By-laws the word ‘‘Channel’’ shall include ‘‘nala’’, ‘‘river’’, 
‘‘stream’’, ‘‘ditch”’ or ‘‘watercourse’’. 


Penalty 


2. Fines.—The penalty for the infringement of any of these by-laws 
shal] be— 


(a) oa fine not exceeding the sum stated at the foot of the by-laws, 


(b) in the case of a second or subsequent conviction for a similar 
offence, a fine not exceeding the sum (if any) stated in that 
behalf at the foot of the by-laws, and 

(c) in the case of a continuing offence, a further fine, not exceeding 
the sum (if any) stated at the foot of the by-law as the daily fine, 
which daily fine may be :mposed for each day after written notice 
of the offence from the Commissioners. 


3. Setting up obstruction.—No person shall, without the general or 
special permission of the Commissioners, set up any obstruction in any 
channel which is a source of public water supply. 

Explanation.—The spreading of fishing nets and the placing of fishing 
traps in any such channel are included in the word ‘‘obstruction” 
98 used in this by-law. 


Fine, Rs, 10; daily fine, Rs. 2. 


4,—-Easing oneself.—No person shall ease himself at the side of or in 


any channel. 
Fine, Rs. 10.

nN .. 


5, Throwing rubbish, sewage or offensive matter.—No person shall 
throw, deposit or বি any rubbish, sewage or offensive matter into 
any channel, tank or well. | 


Fine, Rs. 10, on a second or subsequent conviction Rs, 50. 


6. Cleanliness of banks, and access for .conservancy,.—Every owner or 
oceupier of any part of the bank of any channel which is a source of public 
water supply shall— 


(a) keep such bank free from filth, dense vegetation and other obstruc- 


tion, and 


(b) at all times allow the Commissioners, or any of their servant duly 
authorised in this behalf, to have access to such channel for any 
purpose of public conservancy. 


Fine, Rs. 10. 


7. Weeds.—Any person taking weeds frum a channel or tanks shall 
completely remove them from the slope and crest of such channel or tank 
within three days. 


Fine, Rs. 10; daily fine, Res. 2. 


8. Masonry platforms and drains for wells.—The owner of every well 
which 18 a source of public water supply shall construct a masonry platform 
and drains to prevent the surface water falling into the well or stagnat:ng 
in its vicinity. 

Fine, Rs. 10; daily fine, Rs. 2. 


9. Bathing Or washing near well or standpipe.—No person shall bathe, 
or shall wash clothes, utensils or any other articles, within a distance of ten 
feet from the lowest platform of any well, pump, standpipe or hydrant. 


Fine, Rs. 10, 


10. Use of standpipes and fountains.— Except with the general or special 
permission of the Commissioners and under such conditions as they may 
from time to time prescribe, no fee shall use any standpipe, pump, 
hydrant or fountain belonging to the Commissioners for any purpose other 
than drawing water— 


(a) for drinking on the spot, or 
(b) for carry:ng away for domestic purposes. 
Fine, Rs. 10, 


11. No person shall put his mouth to any tap or cock attached to any 
standpipe or hydrant used by the public. 


Fine, Rs. 10. 


12. No person shall cause damage to any hydrant, standpipe, pump, 
fountain, water tap or cock belonging to the Commissioners or tamper with 
any of their property connected with the waterworks in such a manner as to 
affect the use of public water supply. 


Fine, Rs, 20. 


13. No person suffering from leprosy or any other contagious disease 
shall touch or draw from anv standpipe used by the public. 


Fine, Rs, 20. 
14. Steeping jute, hemp, etc.—No person shall, without the general or 
special permission of the Commissioners steep in any tank or channel] any 


jute, hemp or other vegetable matter which ie likely to render the water 
offensive or noxious to the neighbourhood. 0 


Fine, Rs. 10; on a second or subsequent conviction, Rs. 50.

15. Washing infected articles.—No person shall wash or cause to be 
washed in cr near any tank or channel or any other receptacle for water 
used by the public for drinking or bathing purposes any clothes, bedding or 
other articles which have been used by a person suffering from any infec- 
tious or contagious disease. 

Fine, Rs. 50. 


_ 16. Bathing by infeoted persons.—No person suffering from any infec- 
tious or contagious disease shall bathe in any public bathing place. 


Fine, Ra. 10. 


17. Bathing places reserved for femaies.—No male person above twelve 
years of age shall stand on or near, or bathe or wash in any bathing place 
which has been reserved by the Commissioners at a meeting for the use of 


females only. 
Fine, Rs. 10. 


18. Cattle troughs.—No person shall use for any other purpose any 
pid ea trough which has been reserved by the Commissioners for watering 
cattle.

Closed cess-pools or household septic tanks and soak pits 


30. When any person intends to install a privy or urinal on the water- 
carriage system, and there is no municipal underground sewerage system 


with which it may be connected, he may install such privy or urinal on 


the condition that he provides a covered septic tanks, and a soak pit or a 
disposal gallery in conformity with the provisions of by-law 36, 


31. A covered septic tank shall be constructed in accordance with the 
type design to be kept at the municipal office, together with means for 
disposal of the effluent from the septic tank. 


382. The septic tank shall be constructed of watertight masonry, 
concrete, or earthware, and shall have a capacity of not less than two cubic 
feet per user, the number of users being takeu as the maximum number 
of persons who will ordinarily use the privy or urinal connected to the 


septic tank. 


33. The means for disposal of the effluent of the septic tank shall 
consist of either— | 


(9) a covered soak pit or well, the bottom of which shall be carried 
down to a porous sandy stratum—in any case to a depth of not 
less than two feet below the lowest sulsuii water level. Soak 
pits may be lined or unlined, depending on the nature of the 
upper strata. An unlined soak pit shall be between eighteen 
inches and two feet in diameter and the quality of liquid run 
into it shall not be more than one hundred gallons per day. A 
lined soak pit or well shall have a horizontal cross sectional area 
of not Jess than one square feet for every twenty-five gallons of 
water discharged into it daily ; or ১. ৭ ۱

Vi. MODEL BY-LAWS RECULATING RAC-FLOCK MANUFACTURE 
AND TRADE IN RACS AND BOMES 


1. In these by-laws ‘‘rag-flock’? means flock which has been produced 
wholly or partly by tearing up woven or knitted or felted materials, whether 
old or new, but does not include flock obtained wholly in the process of 
scouring and finishing or newly woven or newly knitted or newly felted 
fabrics, 


2. No person shall sell or have in possession for sale any rag-flock 
manufactured from rags of use for the making of any article of upholstery, 
cushions or beddings, any such flock unless it conforms to the standard 
prescribed below and unless such flock has been disinfected to the satisfac- 
tion of the Commissioners. 


The amount of soluble chlorine (as chlorides removed by thorough 
washing with distilled water at a temperature not exceeding 20 sentigrade 
from not less than 40 grammes of a well-mixed sample of rag-flock shall not 
exceed 30 parts of chlorine in 100,000 parts of the flock. 


. No person shall trade in rags in second hand clothing or bedding, 
unless the Health Officer or the Commissioners are satisfied ubout the 
cleanness 01 such articles and also about the freedom of such articles from 
infection of any dangerous disease. 


4. No person shall trade in bones or products of bomes unless such 
art:cles kave been disinfected before importation or exposure of sale, to the 
satisfaction of the Health Officer or the Commissioners. , 


5. Whoever commits a breach of any of the by-laws 2 to 4 shall be 
punishable with fine which may extend to fifty rupees.

Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Depart- 
ment, by its order No. 6866-I.R./IR/10L-98 /65, dated 
Caloutta, the 27th December 1965, referred an indus- 
trial dispute between Messrs. Paterson Engineering 
Co. (P) Ltd. and their workmen represented by the 
Paterson Engineering Co. Employees’ Union to this 
Tribunal for adjudication on the following issue: 


Whether the termination of service of Shri K.C. 
Sharma is justified?! To what relief, if any, 
is he entitled? 


After service of notice, both parties entered appear- 
ance and filed respective written statements. 


The union in its written statement filed on 21st March 
1966, inter alia, contended that Paterson Engineer- 
ing Oo. (P). Ltd., was engaged in designing, suppling 
and installing water purification plants, water softening 
plant, 960. and employed about 116 workmen in 
Calcutta. The workmen of the company, numboring 
about 80, formed a union in 1963 under the name 
and style of Paterson Engineering Co. Employees’

On 22nd May 1964. the Company wrote to Shri Sharma 
intimating him that his service will not be required as

and he was requested to proceed on 30 days’ privilege 
leave that was due to him. Consequently his service 
must be taken to have been terminated with effect 
from 30th June 1964 on the basis of the letter. dated 
22nd May 1964 (Ext.A.). Sharma replied to this 
letter on 4th June 1964 (Ext.1) challenging the termina- 
tion of his service on the ground that it was passed in 
utter disregard of the provisions of law and in mala- 
fide exercise of power. He requested the management 
to withdraw and cance! the aforesaid notive. The 
Management replied on 16th June 1964 controverting 
the position (Ext. B) and thereafter on 27th July 1964,

The Company repliod to this letter on 10th August

in their letter, dated 10th August 1964 (Ext. A) and 


finally on 25th August 1964 the union wrote to the 


Labour Commissioner whereupon certain conciliation

The objections taken by the company to this refer- 
ence are as follows :— 


(a) The dispute is an individual dispute and not an 
industrial dispute. 


(b) The union was not entitled to excuse the case

(9) Sharma was not a “workman” within the

Disputes Act, 1947. ۱ 


(0) Even assuming that Shri Sharma was a workman 
and the dispute was an industrial dispute, 
termination of service of Shri Sharma being 
a discharge simpliciter made in the bona fide 
exervise of the employer's power, could not” * 
be questioned by the Tribunal. 


I shall take up these objections seriatim. 


(a) It is well settled that a dispute between an em- 
ployer and single employee is not un industrial dispute 
with the m aning of secton 2(k) of the Industrial Dig-

naligt’s Cage reported in A.I.R. 1963, S.C., page 
380 that if a dispute in its inception was an individual 


Union and the said Union was registered on 14th May 
1963. The Company paid very low wages to its 
employees and the general behaviour towards the 
employees was rude and unworthy of a respectable 
institution. One of the important and active members 
of the union Shri K.C. Sharma, a chemist of the com- 
pany, joined the union from its inception. His partici- 
pation in the union was not looked upon by the manage- 
Ment with good grace and the company was on the 
look out for a way to victimise him. On 22nd May 
1964, the company suddenly issued a notice of termina- 
tion of service of Shri Sharma without issuing any charge 
sheet or holding any prior enquiry. Said 0৭101 
terminating the servive of Shri Sharma was palpably

company and finally wrote to the Labour Commissioner, 
Governmont of West Bengal, and a conciliation proceed- 
ing was started. At the said conciliation proceeding 
the company took up the position that it was a case 


of discharge simpliciter and Shri Sharma was not & 


“workman’’, being a member of the supervisory staff, 
drawing more than Rs. 500 per month. The union 
contended that Shri Sharma did not belong to the

simpliciter. The union further asserted that the

The company in their written statement filed on 
2186 May 1966, inter alia, challenged the order of refer- 
ence as ultra vires and invalid and asserted that the 
Tribunal had no jurisdiction to adjudicate the issue 
referred to it. The company asserted that Shri Sharma 
was not a workman, as he was employed in a super- 
visory capacity on a salary exceeding Rs.500 per 
month. The company further asserted that the 
union was not competent to raise any dispute over the 
termination of Shri Sharma’s service as he was not a

dispute being an individual dispute, not supported by 
a body of workmen, could not be regarded as an indus- 
trial dispute. The company further contended that the 
Tribunal has no jurisdiction to go into the matter as 
the termination in the instant case was a case of dis- 
charge simpliciter. 


The union examined four witnesses including Su-

samo year whereupon the Union took up the cause of 
the worker and got the reference made. On a motion

competent to take up the cause of the worker as he was 
not a member of the union on the date of his dismissal 
and the dispute therefore was an individual dispute 

‘and not an industrial dispute, the High Court upheld 
the plea. In the latter case the workman was dis-

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in its Labour Des 
partment, by order No. 217-1.R./IR/7L-20 /65, 
dated 20th January 1967, had referred the following 
industrial digpute between Messrs. Wellington Jute 
Mills, P. O. Righra, district Hooghly (Managing Agents: 
James Finlay & Co., Ltd., 2 Notaji Subhag Road, 
Caleutta-1), and their workmen represented by Jute 
Workers’ Federation, 35B Wollington Street, Calcutta, 
to this Tribunal under section 10 of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act, for adjudication. The issue under reference 


is as follows: 


Is the Management justified in not promoting Shri 
Bagala Chatterjee to 49731180107 “SA” grades 8 
What relief, if any, is he entitled to 1 


After the service of the ugue] notices, both parties 
appeared on 20th February 1967, and filed a joint 
petition of settlement stating that the dispute had been 
amboably settled by thom and prayed for an award in 
terms of the petition of compromise. It appears to 
me that the terms of thy settlement are bona fide, 
légal and proper, and should be given effect to. I 


employee by virtue of power conferred on him by the 
terms of contract. 16 is to be pointed ont that in the 
“Baid case fault of the employee was pointed out to 
her and her performance was not up to the standard. 
In another caso relied on by the learned Advocate of 
the Company reported in 1966-67 (30 F.J.R.), page 442 
the Punjab High Court held that in the absence of a 
standing orders or other contract of service between 
the employer and his workmen the conditions of his 
service were governed by the Delhi Shops and Establish- 
ment Act, 1954, and as the termination of service was 
bona fide and in compliance with the provisions of the 
aforesaid Act, the Industrial Tribunal could not inter- 
fare with the same. This argument has not been 
canvasacd before me nor can the corresponding provision 
of section 15(i) of the West Bengal Shops and Eatablish- 
ment Act, 1963, be said to be attracted to the facta and 
ciroumstances of the present case. That being the 
position and as the Company has failed to assign any 
reagon for the discharge of a permanent workman, the 
Tribunal cannot upheld the termination as a bona fide 
case of discharge simpliciter. On behalf of the Union 
it was sought to be contended that this was a clear 
case of victimisation but on this point the evidence 
cannot be said to be very satisfactory. However for the 
reasons already discussed I must held that this was a 
case of unfair labour practice where the company 
proceeded to terminate the service of a permanent 
employee which thoy were not entitled to do under the 
terms of the contract and the termination cannot also 
be construed as bona fide in the circumstances of the 
caso. It follows therefore that the termmation in the 
instant case must be held to be unjustified and Shri 
Sharma is entitled to be reinstated to his former post. 
As Shri K. C. Sharma _ is out of employment ever since 
the termination of his service he will got full pay and 
allowance from the date of termination of employment 
till the date of his reinstatement. 


This is the award of the Tribunal and #t will become 
enforcoable on the expiry of thirty days from the date of 
its publication in the ‘‘Calcutta Gazotte.” 


Taken at my dictation and corrected by me. 


S. K. BHATTACHARYYA,

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 


Public Health 
NOTIFICATION 


No.  P.H./1881/2R-17/67.—7th April 1967.—Whereas the Governor 15 
Satisfied that the district of Howrah, excluding the mw icipalareas, is threatened 
with an outbreak of small-pox; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 2 of the 
Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (III of 1897), the Governor is pleased to prescribe 
the following temporary regulations for the prevention and control of small-pox 
and for the medical inspection, isolation, observation and surveillance of persons 
suffering from, or suspected of being infected with, small-pox in the said district 
for a period of six months:— 


Temporary Regulations for the Prevention and Control of Small-pox 


1. In these regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject 
or context,— 


(a) “Health Officer” means the Health Officer of the district appointed 
by the State Government, the Chief Medical Officer of Health of 
the district, or the Subdivisional Health Officer of any of the sub- 
divisions of the district within their respective subdivisions; 


(b) “Sanitary Inspector” means a Sanitary Inspector appointed by the 
State Government; 


(c) “Small-pox” means any disease accompanied by an eruption of vesicles 
or pustules;

(৫) “Patient” means a person suffering from or suspected to be suffering 
from small-pox;

(e) “Medical practitioncr’ means any person practising the medical 
profession. 


Notices 


2. If in any case the Health Officer considers that the issue of a notice: 
undcr these regulations is likely to Jead to such an amount of delay as might 
15808116915 the spread of small-pox he may forthwith take such steps as he may 
think fit for carrying out the work, and shall thereafter, as soon as possible, 
issue a notice on the person concerned stating the reasons why such work has 
been carried out. 


3. If any measure which the Health Officer has by a notice issued under 
these regulations, required to be carried out, be not carried out to his satisfaction 
within the time stated in the notice the Health Officer shall be entitled to carry 
out the measure. 


Cost and compensation 


4. (1) All expenses incurred in پت‎ | out রঃ work in pursuance of 
un order issued under these regulations shall be paid by the State Government 
except in any case where the order directs a person to carry out any work in 
relation to property in his possession, in which case the expenses shall be paid 
by such person: 


Provided that where the conditions which 160 the Health Officer to pass 
such an order, are not attributable to any act or default of the person in 
possession of the Property, the State Government may pay to such person 
the whole or a part of the expenses incurred by him in carrying out the order. 


(2) The State Government may recover all expenses incurred by the Health 
Officer in carrying out the measure under regulation 3 from the person or 
persons to whom the notice was originally issued. 


5. The State Government shall pay adequate compensation to any person 
who has sustained substantial loss or damage by reason of anything done’ 
under these regulations: 


Provided that no person shall receive any compensation for anything done 
or suffered under these regulations if he has failed to carry out an order 
issued under these regulations. He shall not direct the patient to be removed 
from the house unless it is, in his opinion, impossible to make proper arrange- 
ments for his isolation therein within the time specified in the order and to 
the satisfaction of the Health Officer. 


Location of disease 


6. When a case of small-pox occurs in a house, the nearest male relative 
in attendance upon the patient, or in the absence of any such relative the 
occupier of the house, or if the occupier be the patient, the senior male inmate: 
of the house other than the patient of the house shall, within twenty-four hours 
of the onset of the disease, give information regarding the occurrence of such 
case either personally or in writing or by means of the chaukidar or 31087. 
village watchman or headman to the nearest Sanitary Inspector. ee 


Part I} THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., APRIL 7, 1967 1109 


7. (1) Every medical practitioner called in to attend upon any case of 
smalJ-pox shall forthwith give notice of the case by a special messenger to the 
nearest Sanitary Inspector or to the Health Officer by post and the cost of such 
messenger in each case shall be defrayed by the State Government. 


(2) The doctor-in-charge of a hospital or a dispensary within the district 
shall forthwith give notice of any case of small-pox brought to such hospital 
or dispensary for treatment to the nearest Sanitary Inspector by a special 
messenger and to the Health Officer by post, and the cost in each case shall be 
defrayed by the State Government. 


8. Thana officers shall supply to the Health Officer such periodical returns 
of cases of small-pox as he may from time to time call upon them to furnish. 


9. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may examine any person 
who is, or suspected to be, suffering from small-pox or who, in his opinion, 
may be infected with or likely to spread smalli-pox. 


Isolation of patients 


10. When the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers that the 
isolation of any patient is a precaution necessary for the protection of the 
neighbouring population, he shall order the patient to observe isolation and may 
order the nearest relative in attendance on the patient, or the occupier of the 
house in which the patient is staying, to arrange for the isolation of the patient 


in such a manner and for such a time as may be approved by the Health 
Officer. 


11. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that any person, 
who has been in contact with a person found to be suffering from small-pox, 
shall be segregated for a period not exceeding a fortnight in a manner and in 
a place to be approved by the Health Officer. 


12. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that any person, 
who has been in contact with a person found to be suffering from small-pox, 
shall be vaccinated or re-vaccinated within a time to be specified in the order. 


13. No person shall enter any place wherein a patient is isolated under 
reguiation 10, without the permission of the Health Officer or a Sanitary 
Inspector. 


14, When a patient has been removed from a house for isolation under 
regulation 10, the State Government shall provide for him free of charge a 
suitable place, with necessary attendants, diet, etc. 


15. No person, who is or has been suffering from small-pox, shall leave 
the place wherc he has been staying until he has received from the Health 
Officer or a Sanitary Inspector written permission to do so. 


16. No person while suffering from evident symptoms of small-pox or in 
the convalescent state of the disease with scabs of pocks on his body shall 
expose himself in any street, road, public place, shop, bazar or any place used 
in common by pcrsons other than members of the family or household to 
which such infected person belongs or shall move from place to place unless 
he is proceeding to a hospital for admission and treatment. 


A110 THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., APRIL 7, 1967 {Part 1 

17. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector authorised by the Health 
Officer in writing in that behalf may, during the prevalence of any outbreak 
of small-pox, order that any bazar, shop or other public place shall remain closed 
for such time as may appear to him to be necessary and may forbid the holding 


of any fair, mela, or other gathering to which people from several villages 
commonly or periodically resort. 


Miscellancous 


18. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may require any person 
to allow to be carried out by such agency and within such time as may be 
کر‎ in the order, such measures for the disinfection of any premises in 
the occupation of such person or for the disinfection or destruction of any 
ef his personal effects, as the said officer or inspector may consider necessary. 


19. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may direct the owner or 
occupier of any premises to take steps to have vaccinated or re-vaccinated 
within a time to be specified in the order any person residing on such premises 
and under the control of such owner or occupier if the Health Officer is of 
opinion that such person has been in contact with any one suffering from 
small-pox. 


20. The Heahh Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may forbid any person 
who has been a patient or who has to his knowledge been in contact with a 
patient to act as vendor of any article for such period as may be specified in 
the order. 


21. No person shall sell any article which has been in contact with a 
patient until it has been disinfected to the satisfaction of the Health Officer or 
a Sanitary Inspector. 


22. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may issue general orders 
that by a specified date certain sanitary precautions of a simple nature such as 
lime-washing of houses, clearing of latrines or the removal of filth or rubbish 
shall be carried ott to his satisfaction. 


23. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may prohibit persons from 
retaining or selling clothes taken from the bodies of persons who have died of 
small-pox and may cause any such clothes to be destroyed. 


24. No person shall carry or permit to be carried in a public conveyance 
a patient except in the case where a patient 1s carried to a hospital with the 
following precautions against spreading the disease, namely:— 


(i) that he is so well covered that the discharge and scabs from the 
lesions do not come directly into touch with the body of the 
conveyance; 


ili) that he is taken to the hospital direct and the conveyance does not 
halt at any other place for transacting any business; and 


(iii) that excepting one or two attendants for the patient no other person 
is carried in the conveyance at the same time. 


25. No person shall expose in any street, shop, bazar or any public place 
any clothing, bedding or other article which has been in contact with a patient 
or shall cause or suffer such articles to be carried in any public conveyance, 


Part I] THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., APRIL 7, 1967 11 
but nothing in this regulation shall apply to a person who transmits any such 


article for the purpose of having the same disinfected with the following 
precautions against spreading the disease:— | 


(i) the article is so well covered with a cloth soaked in strong solution 
of formalin (1 in 400), lysol (1 in 500), izol (1 in 500), or of 
saponified cresol (1 in 160), that it does not come directly in 
touch with the body of the conveyance; 


(ii) the article is taken to the disinfecting station direct and the con- 


veyance does not halt at any other place for transacting any 
business; and 


(iii) excepting one attendant for the purpose of taking the infected articles 
to the disinfecting station no other person is carried in the 
conveyance. 


26. Every conveyance in which a patient or a dead body of a person who 
has died of small-pox or any article that has been in contact with a patient 
is so bese shall be disinfected before it is used again. The disinfection will 
be effectea— 


(i) in the case of a conveyance carrying a patient to hospital, by the 


authorities of the hospital before such conveyance leaves the 
hospital; 


(ii) in the case of a conveyance carrying any clothing, bedding or others 
article of a patient to the disinfecting station, by the authorities 
of such station; and 


(iii) in the case of a conveyance carrying a dead body to the burial or 
cremation ground, by the owner of the conveyance himself and 
such owner shall effect the disinfection with a strong solution of 
formalin (1 in 400), lysol (1 in 500), izol (1 in 500) or of 
saponified cresol (1 in 160). 


27. No person shall carry or permit to be carried in a public conveyance 
the dead body of any person who has died of small-pox without the previous 
written permission of the Health Officer, or a Sanitary Inspector and without 
taking the following precautions against spreading the said disease:— 


(1) the dead body is so well covered with a cloth soaked in a strong 
solution of formalin (1 in 400), lysol (1 in 500), izol (1 in 500), 
or of saponified cresol (1 in 160) that the discharge and scabs 
from the lesions do not come directly into touch with the body 
of the conveyance; 


(ii) the dead body is taken to the burial or cremation ground direct and 
the conveyance does not halt at any other place for transacting 
any business; and 


(iii) excepting attendants for the dead body no other person is carried 
in the conveyance at the same time. 


28. No person shall, without the written permission of the Health Officer, 
dispose of any corpse except by burning or burial. 


29. The Health Officer may approve burning or burial grounds and may 
by order direct either generally or specially in respect to any specified area, 
that corpses shall not be burned or buried at places other than those so 
approved by him.

30. Any person burning or causing to be burnt any corpse shall cause 
the same to be completely reduced to ashes and shall likewise cause the clothes 
or other articles brought with such corpse to be reduced to ashes. 


31. The Health Officer may direct that no person shall bury or cause to 
be buried any corpse, which, in the opinion of the Flealth Officer, is likely 


to spread small-pox, in a grave, not constructed of masonry and less than 
6 feet deep. 


32. The Health Officer may order that no Dome or other person employed 
for the disposal of corpses shall withdraw from his duties without the per- 
mission of the Health Officer unless such Dome or other person has given 


notice in writing not less than one month previously of his intention so to 
withdraw. 


33. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may themselves or through 
any person authorised by the Health Officer or the Sanitary Inspector in that 
behalf seize and dispose of any corpse which in the opinion of the said officer 
or inspector is infected with or is likely to spread small-pox, unless the rclatives 
or friends of the deceased person satisfy him that they are prepared and able 


to dispose of the corpse in a manner which will prevent the spread of 
small-pox. ; 


34. (1) The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may require any: 
person who appears to be acquainted with facts in connection with any case 
or suspected case of small-pox to attend before him at a time to bc stated 
in the order and at any place not more than one mile from the place where 
such person resides or is staying when the order is issued, and such person 
shall appear as so required. 


(2) When the person summoned to appear under paragraph (1) is a female 
who, by the custom of the country, does not appear in public suitable pre-. 
caution shall be taken to respect the said custom. 


35. (1) The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may examine orally 


any person who appears to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances 
of a case or suspected case of small-pox. 


(2) When the person to. be examined under paragraph (1) is a female 
who, by the custom of the country, does not appear in public the officer 
shall take her statement under such conditions as shail admit of due respect 
of the said custom. 


(3) Such person shall be bound to answer questions relating to such case 
put to him or her by such officer, other than questions the answers to which. 
would have a tendency to expose him or her to any criminal charge. 


36. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may, with such assistants 
(if any) as he thinks fit, enter upon any land, or after two hours’ notice in 
writing, into any premises or building used for human habitation at any time 
between sunrise and sunset for the purpose of carrying out any measure or 
making any enquiries authorised by these regulations. 


37. The crew of any inland steam vessel or boat which plies in any canal 
or river and other persons on board such vessel or boat shall be subject to 
these regulations.

OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER 
OF POLICE, CALCUTTA 
ORDER 


To all members of the public in the town of 
Calcutta as defined in section 3 of the Calcutta 
Police Act, 1866 (Bengal Act IV of 1866), and 
in the suburbs of Calcutta as defined by a notifica- 
tion under section IT of the Calecutt: Suburban 
Police Act, 1866 (Benyal Act ا1‎ of 1866), from 

8th April 1967 to the 106 April 1967; 

Whereas, it -is mecessary in order to maintain 
peace and tranquility, to forbid the carrying of fire- 
arms or lethai weapons or aay articles of house- 
hold use which used as a weapon, may provoke, 
annoy or injure human beings excepting weapons 


exempted under Schedule II, item 3(1) of Indian 
Arms Rules, 1962; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of powers conferred 
on the Commissioner of Police under section 144, 
Cr.P.C., read with section 6 of the Caleutta Police 
Act and with section 18, Cr.P.C., I, P. K. Sen, 
Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, hereby prohibit 
euch and every member of the public to carry or 
cause to be carried the said weapons, in the streets, 
roads, lanes, bye-lanes, public parks, mosques, 
temples, gurdwaras, churches or any other place of 
publie worship, amusement or recreation, from the 
Sth April 1967 to 10th April 1967. 


Given under mv hand and seal this 7th duy of 


April 1967. 
Pp. K. SEN, 


Commissioner of Police, Calcutta.

5. (1) Powers of entry, search, seizure, 
etc.—The authorized officer or any officer in the 
Department of Food and Supplies not below the rank 
of Sub-Inspector or any police officer not below the 
rank of Assistant Sub-[nspector or any officer under 
the Regional Director (Food), Eastern Region,

ment and Co-operation (Department of Food), 
Government of India, not below the rank of 
Inspector, may, with a view to securing compliance 
with this Order or to satisfying himself that this 
Order has heen complied with— 


(a) inspect or cause to he inspected any book or 
documents or accounts as well as any 
stocks of rice or paddy belonging to or 
under the control of any person, 


(b) require any person to give any information 
in his possession with respect to any busi- 
ness or undertaking for purchase, sale or 
storage of rice or paddy, 


(c) stop and search forthwith with such aid or 
assistance as may be necessary any person 
or vehicle or vessel or animal used or 
suspected of being used for delivery of rice 
or paddy from a godown or other premises 
where he has reason to believe that rice | 
or paddy is stored, 


(d) enter and search with such aid or assistance 
as may be necessary any such godown or 
other premises, and 


(e) seize and remove with such aid or assistance 
as may be necessary the entire quantity of 
any stock of rice or paddy along with the 
packages, coverings, or receptacles in 
which such stock is found and the animals, 
vehicles, vessels or other convey 8 
used in carrying such stocks, if he hag 
reason to suspect that any provision of — 
this Order has been, is being, or is about 
to be, contravened in respect of such 
stocks or any part thereof or in respect of 
any other stock of rice or paddy which 
immediately before the contravention, was 
stored or possessed along with such stocks 
and thereafter take or authorise the 
taking of all measures necessary for 
securing the production of the stocks of 
rice or paddy, packages, coverings, recep- 
tacles, animals, vehicles, vessels or other 
conveyances so seized in a court of law 
und for their safe custody pending such 
production ; 


Provided that in exercising the powers under this 
sub-paragraph due regard shall be paid to the social

of the place or premises.

paragraph.

AGREEMENT 


MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT made this 
thirteenth day of February, One Thousand Nine 
Hundred and Sixtyseven between The Bharat Battery 
Manufacturing Company (Private) Limited, a Com- 
pany registercd Under Companies Act, 1956 and 
having its registered Office at 238A, Acharya Jagadish 
Chandra Bose Road, Calcuttar20 (hereinafter called 
the “The Company”) of the ONE PART, And the 
GOVERNOR of the State of West Bengal (herein- 
ufter called “The Governor”) of the OTHER PART. 


WHEREAS for the purpose of providing amenities 
to its workmen, the Company has applied to the 
Government of West Bengal for the acquisition under 
the ptovisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 
(hereinafter referred to as the said “Act”), of the 
piece or parcel of land containing more or less 
0.7185 of an acre or thereabout situate in the city 
of Calcutta and more particularly described in the 
Schedule hereto and delineated in the plan* hereunto 
annexed; 


AND WHEREAS the said Government of West 
Bengal (hereinafter referred to as the “Government”) 
upon the advice of the Land Acquisition Committee 
constituted under Rule 3 of the Land Acquisition

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 


MINISTRY OF FOOD, AGRICULTURE, COMMU- 
NITY DEVELOPMENT AND CO-OPERATION 


Department of Agriculture 


NOTIFICATION 
No. 16-43 /58-17. 


New Delhi, the 6th January 1967 
G.S.R.—In exercise of the powers conferred by 
section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (10 
of 1955), the Central Government hereby makes the 
following Order further to amend the Fertiliser 
(Control) Order, 1957, namely:—

trol) First Amendment Order, 1967.‏

1803 Under the said Award dearnces allowances

Tribunul further awarded that the rates of D.A. should

of increase in the cost of living index dearness allowance 
should be increased by Rs. 1 26, Res. 1-35 and Re. 1 -42

Similar adjustments muy be made when coat of living 
index falls, but no adjustment to be made below 160 
points.

09899”, of 26th September 1963. 


After receipt of the order of the Government of 


West Bengal referred to abovo, I fixed 20th of February 
for hearing. As I relinquished the charge of the office

as Director, E. 8. I. (Medical Benefit) Scheme, West 
Bengil, on 17th Febru.ry 1967 I could not hear the

the arbitration despite change in my assignment. 
I fixed 28th of February 1967 for hearing on which 
date the representatives of the workmen turned up but 
none appoared on behalf of the employers. I fixed 
6th March for hearing on which date all the parties 
apperred. On behalf of the owners a request was 
made for four weeks’ time. This was opposod by the 
Unions. As only one issue was involved and as the 
Unions had not 8510. anything new in their statement, 
copy of which was forwarded to the Owners’ Assovia- 
tions on 28th February 1967, I allowed only one week’s 
time. The parties were asked to appear on 13th 
March 1967. Immediately thereafter an application 
wags made on behalf of the employers stating that they 
needed one month’stimo for raising preliminary objec- 


tion against the Arbitration Argecment which they

was strongly opposed by Unions. The Owners’

that the mon have gone on strike protesting against the 
objection petition. On 8th Merch the parties appeared. 
The Owners’ representative Shri Jiten Banerjee, after

need be taken on the petition of objection, which was 
filed on 6th March. The parties thereafter took time

As already stated the Owners have submitted above 
their difficulties. Such difficulties are faced by various 
industries, big or small, where D.A. have also beon 
increased. The workers are also facing the difficulties 
on account of increase in the cost of living index. The 
leather industry on account of devaluation has also 
been partly benefited as is seen in one of the publications 
of “The Tanner”. Taking all these factors into considera- 
tion I award that the existing rates of dearness allow- 
ances for the unskilled, semi-skilled and skilled workers 
be increased by Rs. 11.00, Rs. 12.00 and Rs, 12.50 per 
month r tively. The increases in the aforesaid 
rates shall be with offect from Ist of January 1967. 


I now come to the demand for inoreases in the rates 
of D.A. for 1966, I am not accepting the Owners vontun- 
tions that dearness allowances should not be revised with 
retrospective effect. The issue under reference is not 
limited. It is a fact that the workers did not get any 
increase in D.A. im 1966 on the basis of the average ہ٥۷‎ 


_ of living index of 1965. The parties were negotiating 


but they could not arrive at any settlement. It will 
not be fair to deny some relief for the year 1966 to the 
workmen. The rise in the average cost of living index 
tor 1965 was about 27 points. The industry may find 
it difficult to bear any substantial burden on account 
of increase in the rates of D.A applicable for 1966. 
Taking into account the difficulties of the workers and 


_ the position of the industry J award that the workers

No. 1085-1.R./TR/9L-12/65.—23rd March 19607 issue 


Whether the retirement of Sarbashri Akal Singh 
and Swaparna Singh with effect. from Ist March 
1966 18 justified ? To what relief, if any, ٥ 
they entitled 7 7 


On receipt of the order of reference usual notices 
wero issued on the parties fixing 11th October 1966 for 
their appearance as also for tho filing of written state- 
ment by the union. In pursuance of the notices, parties 
appeared on the date fixed and on union's petititon for 
direating the company to file its written statement first, 
the company was directed to submit its written state- 
ment by [8th January 1966. No written statement 
was, however, filed by the company on that date and 
it took time to file its written statement. Ultimately 
the parties filed a joint petition on Lith February 1966 
stating that the dispute under reference has been 
settled on terms mentioned in the Memurandum of 
Nettlement annexed to the petition and praying for an 
award in terms of the Memorandum of Settlement. The 
joint potition was signed by Shri L. M. Pradhan. General 
Secretary, National Union of Plantation Workers for 
the union and Shri N. R. Dutta, Manager, Kalchini 
Tea Estate for the company. 


I have parused the terms of tho settlement and they 
appear to me quite fair and reasonable—I am satisfied 
that the parties have settled the dixpute on the terms 
mentioned in the Memorandum of Settlement. and that 
there is no existing dispute botween them. The terms 
accordingly recorded and a Compromise award passed. 
The joint petition together with the Memorandum of 
Settlement do form part of the award. 


This is my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me. 
S. K. DATTA GUPTA, 
Judge.

informing her that duc to 0৮978 financial position and 
reorganisation of the club, she had bevsomes urplus, 
und aa such, she was retrenched from the sorvices of the 
elub from 30th November 1965. The plea of adverse 
fin..nvial position cannot be supported becwune the 
leirned Second Industrial Tribunal held that the club 
could bear the burden of the grauity scheme and made 
& scheme for payment of grauity to the  workimen 
on ith February 1066; hence the letter, dated 29th 
November 1965 —Ext. 5—containing the recital that 
duo to the adverse financial position and reorganisation 
of the club Mrs.Gomes had become surplus to tho 
requirement of the club. does not appear to he bons tide. 
Thore is nothing tu show that the club’s tinancial

for the reorganisation of the olub, retronchment of 
Mrs. Gomes was necessary. I accoringly hokl that the 
retrenchment was mala fide. 


Furthermore, there is nothing to show that Mrs. 
Gomes was paid any retrenchment compensation, or 
w. 6 asked to receive payment prior to her retrenchment. 
There is a recital in the letter—Ext. 5—that ‘the 
০11) hereby offers you all your legal dues including one 
m mth’s wages in lieu of notices and retrenchmont 
compensation under the Industrial Disputes Aot.”’ 
There ig only the offer of the club. Section 25F(b) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act provides that no work- 
m -n employed in any industry who has been in continu - 
o: م‎ service for not less than one yoar under an employer 
aliall be retrenched by that employer until he has been 
pid retrenchment compensation which shall be equi- 
vi lent to 15 days’ avorage pay for every completed 
year of service or any part thereof in excess of six 
months. Tho requirement prescribed by section 
25F(b) is a condition precedent br the retrenchment of 
tle worker. The letter—Ext. 5—really amounted to a 
o: ll to receive payment subsequent to retrenchment. 
In view of the ruling reported in 1964(I) L.L.J., 525 
(National Iron & Steel Co., Ltd., and Third Industrial 
Tribunal, West Bengal, and others), I hold that the 
offer is bad and consequently the retrenchment order 
bocomes incompetent. 


I must, therefore, hold that the order of retrenchment 
of Mrs. Elizabeth Gomes passed by the Calcutta Swim. 
ming Club ie illegal and mala fide. The club is therefore 
directed to reinstate Mrs. Elizabeth Gomes without 
interruption of her service and to pay her back wages. 
This order will take effect within one month from the 
dite of publication of this award in the ‘‘Caleutta

BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL

Present : 


Shri S. K. BHATTACHARYYA, Judge, 


Second Industrial Tribunal. 


By order No, 5114-1.R./1R/11L-325/64, dated Cal- 
cutta, the 20th November 1965, Government of West 
Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred an industrial 
dispute between Mesars. The National Sugar Mills Ltd. 
and their workmen represented by the National 
Sugar Mills.Workers’ Union, Bolpur, to this Tribunal for 
adjudication on the following issue : 


Whether the Management is justified in terminating 
the service of Shri Balakram Das? To 
what relief, if any, is he entitled ? 


Findings 


After service of notice on the parties Union filed 
written statement but the company took no steps. 
Subsequently a letter was received from the Official 
Liquidator, High Court, Calcutta, stating that he was 
appointed as a provisional liquidator of the company 
and the company has been finally wound up. He 
took time to file written statement but no written state- 
Ment was actually filed nor any step taken by him. 
Subsequently the Union also failed to appear. No 
sufficient cause for non-appearance was shown by cither 
party and no material was placed before the Tribunal 
to come to a conclusion one way or other on the issue 
framed. In the circumstances the Tribunal proceeds 
under Rule 22 of the Rules and holds that the industrial 
dispute under reference is no longer in existence. The 
Tribunal therefore makes a “no dispute’ award in the 
Instant case. 


Dictated and correated by me. 
S. K. BHATTACHARYYA,

WHEREAS it is expedient to amend the Bengal Finance Ben. Act 
(Sales Tax) Act, 1941 for the purposes and in the manner ۲٣ ০৫94৫. 
hereinafter appearing;

follows:— 
Ghort title 1. (J) This Act may be called the Bengal Finance (Sales 
حت قح‎ = Tax) (Amendment) Act, 1967. 
emt. (2) It shall be deemed to have come into force on the

ment کہ‎ 1941 (hereinafter referred to as the said Act),— 

Ben. Act 2) in clause (c) of sub-section (7), for the words

shall be substituted;

ORDER 


No. 2649-F.S. /FS/142-83 /67.—18th April 1967.—Whereas the Governer 
is of opinion that it is necessary and expedient so to do for maintaining 
supplies of rice and for securing its equitable distribution and availability 
at fair prices in West Bengal; | 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the 
Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1965) and, in particular by sub- 
section (3B) thereof, read with the Government of India, Ministry of Food, 
Agriculture, Community Development and Co-operation (Department of 
Food), order No. G.S.R. 906, dated the 9th June 1966, as subsequently 
amended, the Governor is pleased to make, with the prior concurrence of 
the Central Geverpmynt,, the following Order, namely :— 


1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(1) This Order may be 
called the West Bengal Rice Mills (Levy) Order, 1967. 


(2) It extends to the whole of West Bengal. 
(3) It shall come into force at once. 


2. Definitions.—In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) ‘Director’? means the Director of District Distribution, Procure- | 
ment and Supply, in the Department of Food and Supplies, 
Government of West Bengal, and includes all District Con- 
trollers, Additional District Controllers and Assistant District |. 
Controllers of - Food and Supplies in the Department of Mood — 
and Supplies; 


(b) “Food | Corporation’” means the Food Corporation of: India 
established under the Food Corporations Act, 1964 (37 of 1904), 


acting as an agent of the Government for the purposes of this 
Order ; -"

(c) “Government’’ means the Government of the State of West 
Bengal ; 


(d) ‘‘Licensed miller’? means the owner of # rice mill within the 
meaning of section 8 of the Rice-Milling Industry (Regulation) 
Act, 1908 (21 of 1958), duly licensed under the provisions of 
that Act, who purchases pa 7 for willing rice and sells the 
rice produced out of such paddy; 


(৬) ‘‘procurement price’? means, in relation to any variety and grade 
of rice, the price specified in thia Order for such variety and 
grade having regard to the price prevailing during the post- 
harvest period in respect of such variety and grade of rice; 


(1) ‘‘rice’’ means rice produced or manufactured with the aid of power 
and includes broken rice (khud) but does not include chira, 
muri or khoi; 


(gz) ‘‘rice mill’? means a rice mill as defined in clause (8) of section 
3 of the Rice-Milling Industry (Regulation) Act, 1958 (21 of 
1938) ; 


(h) ‘Schedule’? means a Schedule appended to this Order, 


3. Levy on rice produced in a rice mill.—(1) Every licensed miller 
shall sell to the Director or the Food Corporation the entire quantity 11 
rice produced or manufactured in any rice mill out of paddy owned by hin 
and held by him at the date of commecement of this Order, 


(2) Every licensed miller shall sell to the Director or the Food Corpora- 
tion 100 per cent. of the quantity of rice produced or manufactured in any 
es tam out of paddy owned by him after the date of commencement of 
this Order. 


(3) Any rice required to be sold under sub-paragraph (1) or sub- 
paragraph (2) shall be delivered to, and paid for at the appropriate 
procurement price by, the Director or such Officer of the Government in 
the Department of Food and Supplies not below the rank of Inspector or 
7001) agent of the Government as may be authorised in this behalf by the 
Director of District Distribution, Procurement and Supply, or such officer 
or agent of the Food Corporation as may be authorised in this behalf by 
the Food Corporation, by general or special order, to take delivery and 
make payment on behalf of the Director or the Food Corporntion, as the 
case may he. 


4. Procurement prices.—(1) For purposes of this Order, the procure- 
ment prices of different varieties and grades of rice shall, subject to the 
provisions of sub-pnragraphs (2) and (3), be as follows :— 


Variety. Grade. Rate per quintal. 
Ra. 
Aman rice (i) Common 93:75 
(ii) Fine 97-80 
(iii) Superfine 101 -80 
Aus and Boro rice All grades 93 -75 


(2) The rates specified m sub-paragraph (1) are in each case for net 
weight of bagged grain and include the cost of new gunny bag containers 
and of weighing, bagging, sewing, marking and handling for delivery; 
where gunny bag is supplied by the Director or the officer or agent 
authorised to take delievery under sub-paragraph (3) of paragraph 3, the 
rates shall be reduced by Rs. 2.25 per quintal; and where no weighing, 
bagging, sewing, marking or handling is done by the seller, the rates shall 
le reduced by 16 paise per quintal. 


(3) The rates specified in sub-paragraph (1) are for rice of fair average 
quality conforming . to the specifications given in Schedule I; for rice 
below the fair average quality the rates shall be reduced by the amounts 
of cuts indicated in column 4 of that Schedule. 


_ &Explanations.—(1) ‘Aman rice’’ includes all varieties of rice produced 
in or Imported into West Bengal other than rice of aus and boro varieties.

(2) 00101000782, in relation to grades of aman rice, includes all grades of 
aman rice other than fine and superfine grades. 


(3) ‘‘Fine’’? and ‘Superfine’, in relation to the grades of aman rice, 
mean respectively the موا‎ of aman rice specified in columns 2 and 3 of 
Schedule II and include similar grades. 


5. Certain restrictions on milling by licensed millers.—-No licensed 
miller shall produce or manufacture in his rice mill muri rice out of paddy 
owned by him, except under and in accordance with a permit granted by the 
Jhirector. 


Explanation.—In_ this paragraph, the expression “muri rice’? means 
rice which is produced or manufactured exclusively for making muri 
therefrom. 


6. Power of the Director to require licensed millers to mill paddy held 
by them.—The Director may, if he considers it necessary and expedient so 
to do, direct any licensed miller to effect milling of rice of, or eonvert into 
rice, the whole or a_ specified part of the stock of paddy held by such 
licensed miller in such manner, within such period and in such circumstances 
as may be specified in the direction. 


7. Powers of entry, search, seizure, ete.—(1) The Director or any 
other officer of the Department of Food and Supplies not below the rank 
of Sub-Inspector authorised by the Director or any police officer not below 
the rank of Assistant Sub-Inapector may, with a view to securing com- 
pliance with this Order or to satisfying himself that this Order has been 
complied with— 


(a) imspect or cause to be inspected any book or document or accounts 
as well as any stocks of rice or paddy belonging to or under 
the control of 0 licensed miller; 


(b) require any person to give any information in his possession with 
respect to any undertaking or business for production or 
manufacture of rice or for purchase, sale or storage for sale of 
rice or paddy; 


(9) stop and search forthwith with such aid or assistance as may be 

necessary any person or vehicle or vessel or animal used or 
رو وبا‎ of being used for delivery of rice or paddy from a rice 
mill or other premises where he has reason to believe that rice 
or paddy is stored; 


(d) enter and search with such aid or assistance us may be necessary 
any such rice mill or other premises; 


(e) seize and remove with such aid or assistance as may be necessary 
any stock of rice or paddy along with the packages, coverings 
or receptacles in which such stock is found and the animals 
vehicles or vessels used in carrying such stock, if he has reason 
to suspect that any provision of thie Order has been, is being 
or 18 01006 to be, contravened in respect of such stock or any 
part thereof or in respect of any other stock of rice or paddy 
which, immediately before the contravention, was stored along 
with such stock, and thereafter take or authorise the taking of 
all measures necessary for securing the production of the stocks 
of rice or paddy, packages, coverings, receptacles, animals, 
vehicles, vessels, so seized, in a court and for their safe custody 
pending such production. 


(2) The provisions of sections 102 and 103 of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1898 (5 of 1898), relating to search and seizure shall, so far 
as may he, apply to searches and seizures under this paragraph. 


8. Power to exempt in special cases.—If the Government, having 
regard to the conditions prevailing in any area, considers it necessary or 
expedient so to do in the public interest, it may, by notification in the 
‘Official Gazette’, exempt, subject to such conditions as it may think fit 
to impose, such class or classes of licensed millers in that urea as it may 
apecify in the notification from the operation of all or any of the provisions 
of this Order.

No. 1196-I.R./IR/1A-1(D)/65.—31st March 1967. 
— Whereas the Governor is satisfied that the public 
interest requires that the Inland Water Transport 
Industry in West Bengal, being an industry in 
transport for the carriage of passengers or goods by 
water, should be declared to be a public utility 
service; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-clause (vi) of clause (n) of section 2 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
Governor is pleased hereby to declare the Inland 
Water Transport Industry in West Bengal to be a 
public utility service for the purposes of the said 
Act for a period of six months with effect from the 
4th April 1967. 


No. 1206-1.R./IR/1A-1(F)/65. — 3lst March 1967. 
——Whereas the Governor is satisfied that the public 
interest requires that the service in hospitals and 
rdispensaries should be declared to be a public utility 
Service; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-clause (vi) of clause (n) of section 2 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
Governor is pleased hereby to declare the service in 
hospitals and dispensaries to be a public utility 
Service for the purposes of the said Act for a period 
of six months with effect from the 19th March 1967. 


By order of the Governor, 
A. K. BHATTACHARYYA, Dy. Secy.

Plant Protection Scheme 
RESOLUTION 


No. 1986-PPS, — 28th March 1967. —- For imple- 
menting the programme of purchase of  differcnt 
kinds of pesticides and fungicides to be used for 
plant protection purposes and also with a view to 
reviewing the performance of the plant protection 
equipments purchased under the scheme for plant 
protection, the Governor is pleased hereby to 
constitute a State Plant Protection Committee 
consisting of the following persons: 


(1) Additional Director of Agriculture, West 
Bengal—Chairman. 


(2) Joint Director of Agriculture (Research), West 
Bengal—Member-Secretary. 


Members 


(3) Joint Director of Agriculture (Extension), 
West Bengal. 


(4) Mycologist, West Bengal. 
(5) Entomologist, West Bengal. 
(6) Project Executive Officer, I.A.D.P., Burdwan. 


2. The functions of the’ above Committee among 
other things, will be as follows: 


(i) To judge the efficacy and economics of the 
uses of new products of pesticides and 
fungicides, especially the costly ones, keep- 
ing in view the purchasing capacity of the 
cultivators; 


(ii) to advise on the purchase of new varieties 
of pesticides and fungicides after gaining 
sufficient experience about their effective- 
ness in the fields; ۱ 

(iii) to select new products of pesticides and 
fungicides for tests in different Government 
farms of varying agro-climatic regions; 


(iv) to recommend purchase of costly pesticides 
and fungicides only after giving a fair trial 
in fields for ascertaining accurately their 
effectiveness in protecting crops from pests 
and diseases; 


(v) to apply the knowledge and experience of 
both the Extension and the Research Wings 
and to utilise them in the programme for 
purchase of pesticides and fungicides; 


(vi) to review of the performance of plant protec- 
tion equipments purchased under the Plant 
Protection Scheme. 


Order 


Ordered that the resolution be published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette” and that copies thereof forwarded 
fo the Chairman and the members of the Committee. | 

Ordered also that a copy of the resolution be 
forwarded to all other Departments of this Govern- 
ment, the Director of Agriculture, West Bengal, the 
Chief Engineer (Agri.), and ex-officio Director ]ہ:‎

of generation of thermal power and its resources and

categories of workmen contribute to the prosperity and 
reputation of the company. The workmen of the

ar a condition of service and the service of all the

contention of the union was negatived by the Hon’ble

cannot as such be canvassed again. It now remains 
to be seen if the workers are entitled to any cuetomary 
pujah bonus in the instant case,

The Government of West Bengal, in the Labour 
Department, by its order No. 6632-I.R./IR/8L-4) /60, 
dated Calcutta, the 29th November 1962, referred an 
industrial dispute between Shree Mahaluxmi Cotton 
Mills, P.O. Bengal Enamel, Palta, and their workmen 
ropresented by Shree Mahaluxmi Cotton Mille Employees, 
union to this Tribunal for adjudication on the following 


issue 3 


Are the employees of the Shree Mahaluxmi Cotton 
Mills entitled to get any customary puja bonus ? 
If so, at what rate and on what basis ? 


After receipt of the roference, notices were issued 
upon the parties, who enteped appearance and filed 
separate written statements. The question of puja 
bonus has been the subject-matter of an earlier reference 
before anothor Tribunal and it was held therein that the 
workmen are entitled to two months’ puja bonus as 
a condition of service. This matter went up to the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal and the High Court on a 


petition by the company. 


The Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Ltd., came to be incor- 
porated in the year 1938 and was run under the Managing 
Agency of Messrs. H. Dutta & Others Ltd. In January 
1965, the company was ordered to be wound up by an 
order of the High Court and an interim liquidator 
was appointed. In November 1955 the interim 
liquidator was appointed receive: to run the mills and 
from 1956 to 2nd April 1960. Receiver was in charge 
of the Mills. Meanwhile in July 1959, officia! liquidator 
was directed to sell the mill to the high bidder and on 
18th March 1960, Moesers. Gajra} Pannalal Ltd. pur- 
chased the mills and the eale war duly confirmed. 
On 2nd April 1960, the liquidator served a notice of 
termination of service on the existing employees and 
made over possession of the mills to the purchaser. 
On 5th April 1940 the employees were directed to 
appear before the new purchaser and resume work. 
Thereafter in July 1960 the employees applied before the 
Hon'ble Court for certain benefits. On 30th August 
1960, the employexs applied to the company for pujah 
bonus. Meanwhile bonus appears to have been paid 

- by tho liquidator from 1955 to 1958 and in 1961 present 
‘management made ex-gratia payment of 15 days’ basio 
wago. In 1962 in course of a conciliation proceedings, 
20 days’ basic pay was agreed to be paid as -pujah 
advance, to be deducted in instalments and finally an 
ayroement was reached to refer the matter to a Tribunal 
for an adjudication on the issue of customary pujah 
bonus. The matter was originally heard by my pre- 
decessor, who by his award, dated 9th June 1964, 
found that the workmen were ontitled to one month's 
basic pay as pujah bonus as a condition of service and 
made an award’ accordingly. The company thereupon 
moved the Hon'ble High Court under Article 226 of 
the Constitution, obtained a Rule which was made

In the above cited case bonus was paid unconditionally 
at the samo rate for last 3 years and at a different rate 
the first two years. In 1959 the bonus was paid ex- 
gratia under the terms of settlement and was accepted 
as such by the concerned workmen. For two years 
such bonus was directed to be adjusted againat the profit 
bonus of the recent previous yeara and the terms of 
settlemont further provided that it would be paid to 
those workmen only who had completed 240 days of 
work by the date of payment. The Supreme Court 
held that in the case of customary traditional bonus 
there could not be any such condition and a customary 
or traditional bonus connected with festival has to be 
paid to all workers, irrespective of number of days 
they might have worked before the festival in the years 
jn question and such payment could not be taken into 
aocount an it was made and accepted as ox-gratia pay- 
ment and was hedged with conditions. Moreover, 
there was & break in the pujah bonus for the Jast two 
years which wes sought to be adjusted agaist the 
profit bonus of the previous year. The Supreme Court 
on these facts set aside the finding of the Tribunal 
that the payment of customary or traditional bonus 
on the occasion of the pujah festival had beon established. 
In the case of Tulshidas Khimji, reported in 1962 (1) 
L.L.J., page 435 Supreme Court held that a claim for a 


‘ customary bonus may be negatived on proving that the 


payment was made ex-gratia and accepted as such or 
that it was unconnected with any such occasion as 
festival. 


In the instant 0959 the payment for the year 1961 
was admittedly made ex-gratia and those for the years 
1960 and 1962 was by way of advance. This is also 
admitted by the union's witness Satyendra Nath 
Chakraborty (P.W.1) but he denied that the amounts 
were recovered. Having regard to the state of evidence 
on record, it cannot be held that the tests laid down by 
the Supreme Court in Grahams Trading Company’s 
case cited above have been fulfilled in the instant 0897 
and that being the position, the employees of Shri 
Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills in my view arc not entitled 
to get any customary pujah bonus. 


In the next place Shri Chakraborty contended that 
after the new management took over the establishment, 
the employees stood retrenched and were, thereafter, 
re-appointed; as such the question of their bemg bound 
to pay any customary pujah bonus did not arise 
in the instant case. Messrs. Gajraj Pannalal, it appears, 
purchased the land, building and machineries under 
orders of High Court free from obligations and took over 
possession in April 1960. The Union’s petition, dated

show that the employees are not entitled to claim any 
customary or traditional pujah bonus from the new 
management. The employees also treated their 
appointment as new appointment, for they moved the 
Hon’ble Court on 19th July 1960 for certain retrench- 
ment benefits (vide annexure B to the company’s 
written statement and the order Ext. 0). It would 
thus appear that some of the employees .moved' the

That being the position, the Tribunal is required to 
adjudicate whether on the evidence adduced, ٢ case of 
customary pujeh bonus exists. A customary or tradi- 
tional payment in the nature of pujah bonus was 
distinguished by the Supreme Court from 00182 
bonus as an implied term of employment in Graham 
Trading Company (India) Ltd., caso reported in 1959 
(11) 1,140.) page 303 where it was held that when the 
quostion of customary or traditional bonus arises for 
adjudication, the Tribunal will 11559 to considor : 


(1) Whether the payment has been over an unbroken 
series of years; 


(2) Whether it has been given for a suflivient long 
period though the length of the poriod may 
dopend on the cironmstanves of cach case; 


(3) Tho circumstances that the payment depended 
upon the carnings of profit would have to be 
exoluded und therefore it must be shown that 
payment was made in the years of loss ; and 


(4) The payment must have been at an uniform rate 
throughout to justify an inference thet the 
payment at such and such rate had become 
customary and traditional in the particular 
concern. 

It will bo noticed that the tests laid down were more 
stringent than the tests to be applied for proving a 
pujeh bonus as an implied term of employment as laid 
down in Ispahani Ltd.'s case reported in the same 
volume at page 4. In tho B. N. Ellias Co,’s case 
reported in 1960 (IT) L.L.J., page 290, Supreme Court 
observed that there could be no customary bonus ax 
stich unoonnected with some featival. The subject of 
customury and festival bonus however came 10 bo 
further considered by the Supreme Court in tho 
fegetably Produots cage reported in 1805 (I) 17405 
page 468, where it was laid down that the payment of 
such bonus must be made even in the years of loss 
provided there have been years of loss in the mean time. 
As to uniformity of rates, Suprenie Court observed that 
it did not mean that uniformity should be established

Hon'ble Court and obtained some orders on the footing 
that their employment stood terminated. The 
present management after taking over possession 
introduced a new Standing Orders as the transfer 
was under orders of the High Court and 
not a voluntary one. Notice Ext. C., dated 2nd 
Apri] 1960, by the liquidator and Ext. 4, 
dated 5th April 1980, by the present management 
as also the application for employment by P.W.1 
Satyondra Nath Chakraborty (Ext.A) clearly indicate 
that the services of the employees were treated as 
fresh employment after termination of the old one. 
There is nothing on record to show that the employees 
were taken in with all their past benefits. Moreover, 
there was a break in their service during the period from 
2nd to Sth April 1960, during which period the mill 
did not function. This fact was, of course, disputed 
on behalf of the union but this is clearly proved by 
Ext. C and Ext. 4 and the evidence of the liquidator’s 
men before the Tribunal. The decision of the 
Supreme Court cited on behalf of the union in Dahinga- 
para Tea Estate and Kays Construction Co. (P) Ltd., 
reported in 1958 (11) L.L.J. pages 498 and 660 are not to 
the points. On the contrary the decision in Ispshani 
Ltd.’ case reported in 1059 (IT) L.L.J. page 4 seems to 
be more appropriate. In that case the business of a 
company including its good-will, trade rights, properties, 
asscts, etc., were taken over by another company and 
the service of the workmen of the old company were 
treated as having been terminated and their 
acoounta with the company including their provident 
fund dues and arrear salaries were settled. Such work- 
men were entertained in service by the new company 
without giving any express or implied undertaking 
regarding their continuity in service and the Supreme 
Court in the ociroumstanccs held that the concerned 
workmen were not entiticd to claim continuity of service. 
Tn the instant case Messrs. Gajraj Pannalal purchased 
the undertaking free from all obligations from the 
liquidator under orders of the High Court ond _ the 
official liquidator by his notice (Ext. C.) informed all 
the employees that their serviccs under the liquidator 
shall cease on and from the date of the notice and the 
wages due to the employees would be paid by a certain 
date. These circumstances normally make out that 
there was no continuity in service and the workers, 
as such are not entitled to claim any benefits, if any 
existed from before, even if it be assumed that they 
were otherwise entitled to customary or traditional 
pujah bonus in ‘the instant case. ~ 


From what bas been stated above, it follows that 
the issue must be answered in the negative and the 
employees of Shree Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills are not 
entitled to get any customary pujah bonus. This is 
the award of the Tribunal. 


Taken at my dictation and correoted by me. 
8. K. BHATTACHARYYA, Judge.

INTERIM AWARD 


By order No. 392)-1.R./1R/10L-59/86, dated the 30th 
September. 1966, the Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department, referred under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act and industrial dispute between 
Measra. Babcock & Wiloox of India Lid., and thoir 
workmen represented by Babcock & Wilcox Employees’ 
Union, to this Tribunal for adjudication. The issue 
involved is— 


“Whether rotirement of Shri A. K. Ghosh, Chief 
Clerk and. Cashier and subsequently desig- 
nated. as Chief Cashier from Ist August 
1966 is justified ؟‎ To what relief, if any, 
is he entitled ?” 


The Company and the Union appeared and filed their 
respective statements in response to the notices issued 
on them by the Tribundl. 


By a potition filed on 15th March 1967 the Union 
prayed for interim relief. It is prayed that the Tribunal, 
in an interim award, might direct the Company to pay 
Shri Ghosh three months’ wages and Provident Fund 
dues immediately without prejudice to his right in 
the present proceeding. The Company filed a written 
objection on 17th March 1967. 


The Company has terminated the services of Shri 
A. K. Ghosh on ground of superannuation. The letter, 
dated 20th July 1966, written by the Secretary of the 
Company to Shri Ghosh, which is Annexure B to the 
Union’s present application, shows that the Company 
sent a cheque for Rs. 3,115°14P. in settlement of bis 
salary in lieu of notice of termination of service on 
ground of superannuation. Shri Ghosh accepted the 
cheque under protest and without any prejudice, 
as would appear from his letter, dated 18th July 1966 
(Annexure A to the سن‎ application). The fact 
that the Company offered three months’ salary in 
liou of notice to Shri Ghosh is also admitted in the poti- 
tion of objection filed by the Company on 17th March 
1967. The Union prays that Shri Ghosh may be 
permitted to encash the cheque and to have his provi- 
dent fund dues immediately without any prejudice to 
his rights. 


The learned Advocate for the Company contend, 
that the Company has taken the objection that 
Shri Ghosh is not a “workman” and, accordirgly 
the reference is bad, and hence no interim relief oan 
be given by the Tribunal for want of jurisdiction. 
There is, however, no application by the Company for 
deciding the question of jurisdiction as a preliminary 
point. It has been held in the case of National Tobacco : 
Co. of India Ltd. reported in 1952 L. A. C. 251 that in 
order to pass an interim award it is not necessary 
that the question of jurisdiction must be _ finally 
decided. It is enough if a prima facie case, which 
would not operate to the prejudice of the final 
decision, is made out. 


In the instant case it is the Company itself which 
has offered three months’ wages to Shri Ghosh. If 
the Company be ultimately successful in the case, 
still Shri Ghosh will be entitled to accept this amount 
of three months’ wages which the Company, according 
to its own case, wae bound to pay him in lieu of notice 


208 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 20, 1967 


I, accordingly, pass a ‘no dispute”’ award and dispose 
of the case accordingly. 


Dictated anc corrected by me. 


L.C. BANERJEE, 
Judge. 


L. C. BANERJEE, Judge, 
Fifth lodustrial Tribunal.
