পর سے‎ ee ne i CEE Ee کدو٘ھےم‎ নি ہے‎ ew সত উজ লস. وو سم سس ہے‎ আন سس‎ ০ 


However, I um satisfied that Shri Shaw was appoin- 
ted on probation from 15৮ March 1964 and that he 
was never contirmed in his service. 


There is no dispute before me that the proba- 
tionary period of Shri Pannalal Shaw was extended. 
ln this connection I have gone through the Stand- 
ing Orders prevalent in the Company. Those orders 
have been marked Ext. D. Clause 3 of the Stand- 
ing Orders relates to the classification of workmen. 
In this clause, probationers, temporary and perma- 
nent employees have been defined. According to 


the Standing Orders, 3 permanent workman is one 


who has been engaged on a permanent basis and 
who has satisfactorily completed a probationery 
period of six consecutive months. And ultimately 
couiirmed in writing as permanent. There is also 
provision that the period of probation can be exten- 
ded. In the present case, however, as I have 
already indicated, Shri Pannalal Shaw was appoin- 
ted on probation and. the probationery period was 
at first extended for six months more. Nearabout 
the end of the extended period, the Company wrote 
a letter to Shri Shaw on 27th February 1965 /2nd 
March 1966 informing him that during the period 
of probation for about a year his services and works 
had not been found satisfactory. The Management, 
however, decided to give a final chance to Shri Shaw 
for. improvement of his works by extending the 
period of probation. This extension, there is no 
doubt, was accepted by Shri Shaw. Naturally this 
extension started from 196 March 1965. At the 
beginning of August 1965, the Company wrote 
another Jetter to Shri Shaw informing him that in 


. apite of the extension of the period of probation, he 


could not improve his work and attendance.and that 
he was found very irregular and negligent. In this 
letter the Company mentioned the unauthorised 
periods of absence of Shri Shaw during the last 12 
months. The Company ultimately informed Shri 
Shaw in this letter that due to the unsatisfactory 
work and absence of Shri Shaw, his service was ter- 
minated with immediate effect. The letter is dated 
7th August 1965 and it has been marked Ext. C. 
The period of probation was, however, to come to an 
end with the expiry of August 1965 but the Com- 
pany offered Shri Shaw one month’s wages in lieu 
of notice. 


_ The contention of the Union before me is that the 
Company alleged some misconducts against Shri 
Shaw while terminating his service and as such, the 
Company should have held a domesti¢ enquiry. In 
the present case, the Company has not dismissed 
Shri Shaw. It is a simple termination of service 
on the ground that the Company was not satisfied 
with the works and attendance of the employeo 
during the period of probation. It has been argued 
that it 1s 0, case of colourable exercise of the powers 
by the Company in order to victimise Shri Shaw. 
In the present case, there is no evidence from the 
side of the Union that Shri Shaw became absent 
occasionally on medical grounds. The chart show- 
ing unauthorised absence of Shri Shaw for about 
a year during the period of probation could not be 
validly challenged by the Union. The absence of 
Shri Shaw has been further correborated by the 
attendance register filed in this case. Moreover, 
admittedly according to the Standing Orders, Shri

2nd March 1965, the Company informed Shri Shaw 
that his work had not been found satisfactory and 
in reply to the letter the workman denied the alle- 
gation. Ultimately, however, the Company by its 
letter, dated 7th August 1965, discharged Shri 
Shaw from service on ground of unsatisfactory work 
and unauthorised absence. The Union raised objec- 
tion and ultimately the present industrial dispute 
has been sent to this Tribunal for decision. The 
case of the Union is that the termination of service 
of Shri Shaw was improper and illegal and that 2৮ 1s 
a colourable exercise of the power conferred upon 
by the Management without any bona fides. 


To be brief, the case of the Company as stated 
in its written statement is that the Order of Refer- 
ence is bad as the Union has got no locus-stand to 
represent the workman of the Company. Besides 
this technical objection, it has been stated by the 
اش‎ that Shri Pannalal Shaw was appointed 
as a probationer fitter on lst March 1964, purely on 
a temporary busis. During the period of probation, 
his services were found unsatisfactory. He was 
very irregular in 1855 attendance and his work was 
also not satisfactory. He was given verbal warn- 
ings several times without any effect. Although 
his services deserved to be terminuted, the Manage- 
ment decided to give a further chance to improve 
his work and attendance and extended the period 
of probation. Inspite of the chance, Shri Shaw 
could not improve his attendance or work and ulti- 
mately the Management did not confirm him in his 
service but terminated his service by a letter, dated 
7th August 1965. According to the Company this 
is not 0 case of pure termination of service but a 
case of not confirming o probationer in service 
whose work and attendance were not found satis- 
factory. The Company has, however, denied -the 
naterial allegations. 


Several documents have been exhibited on both 
the sides. On the side of the Union three witnesses 
have been examined while the Company has 
examined only one. 


During evidence Shr} Pannalal Shaw wanted to 
suy that he was not a probationer but a permanent 
employee from the very beginning. He has pro- 
duced one identity card which according to him 
indicates that he was a permanent employee. As 
aguinst this evidence O.P.W. 1, the Manager (Per- 
sonnel) of the Company has been examined. He 
has stated that Shri Pannalal Shaw was a proba- 
tioner and that he was never confirmed. He has 
also stated that the identity card produced by the 
dismissed workman was not meant particularly for 
the permanent employees. I have seen the identity 
card and nowhere has it- heen stated there that the 
card was meant for permanent employee. More- 
over, the most important document has been exhi- 
bited in this case. That is the application for 
employment signed by Shri Shaw. This is Ext. A. 
On this application it is clearly stated by the 
Management that Shri Shaw was appointed on pro- 
bation with effect from lst March 1964. Shri Shaw 
could not challenge this application. Shri N. D. 
- Srimani, appearing on behalf of the Union, does not 
also seriously contend that Shri Shaw was originally 
@ppointed o permanent hand by the Company.

Shaw was initially appointed as probationer for six 
months. ‘or a period of six months more the pro- 
bationery period was extended. The Company was 
not satisfied at the work of Shri Shaw during this 
eriod. The Company could have easily discharged 
bri Shaw but still the Company gave a last chance 
on 2nd of March 1965. This was certainly a good 
gesture and sign of sampathy from the side of the 
Company. There is no evidence that against the 
allegation made in the letter Ext. B, Shri Shaw 
ever protested or that he had any reasonable ground 
to refute the remark made by the Management. 
Thereafter more than 5 months passed, but the 
Company ws not satisfied because in spite of warn- 
ings, there had been no improvement on the side of 
the employee in question. In the facts and 
circumstances of the present case, there can be no 
doubt that the Management gave sufficient opportu- 
nity to Shri Shaw to improve his works and atten- 
dance but Shri Shaw failed rather he did not pay 
proper heed to the warnings given to him. Conse- 
quently the Management had no other alternative 
but to terminate his service without confirming him. 
The Management is ordinarily not bound to give 
reasons in details for the discharge of a probationer. 
In the present cuse, as I have already stated, the 
reasons have been given by the Management as to 
why Shri Shaw was discharged and I find that those 
reasons are proper and valid. The action taken by 
the Management was bona fide and reasonable. It 
should be noted that this is not a case of misconduct 
during the period of probation. Had it been such 
a case, the (oats should have to held an enquiry 
against the misconduct and dismissed him from 
service, ‘That question however, does not arise 
here. I have given my best consideration to the 
evidence of Shri Shaw and the General Secretary. 
I have. also gone through the evidence of the 
Manager 0.۲۰۷۷۰ 1. Of course the evidence of 
P.W. 3 is not of any importance. I fully rely upon 
the evidence of 0.P.W. 1 and reject the evidence of 
P.W.s land 2. According to my finding the 
Management of the Company was justified in not 
confirming Shri Shaw in his service but it acted 
properly to terminate his service very reasonably on 
the ground that the attendance and the works of 
Shri Shaw were unsatisfactory in his probationery 
period. The issue is, therefore, decided in favour 
of the Company and against the Union. Shri 
Pannalal Shaw is not entitled to any relief. | 


Before I close I should mention that at the time 
of argument no question was raised from the side 
of the Company challenging the status of the Union 
to represent the workman of the Company. I am 
satisfied that {his was an industrial dispute.

No. d,-and ou the findings of the Enquiry Officer, 
management dismissed both the workers. It is 
now said by both the workers that the dismissal 
on the basis of the enquiry proceedings, was 
unjustified in us much as the proceedings had 
violated the priuciples of natural justice. If this 
contention of the workers was correct or if the 
evidence at the enquiry even if believed to be true, 
was not sufficient for a prima facie case in support 
of the charges against the workers, this Tribunal 
will certainly interfere with the action taken by 
the management on the findings of the Enquiry 
Officer; otherwise not. It is now’well-established 
principle that in such cases the Tribunal has very 
limited jurisdicaton and will not interfere with the 
findings of the Enquiry Officer or the action of the 
management on the findings of the Enquiry Officer 
if it finds that from the evidence before him the 
Enquiry Ofticer was justified to draw a conclusion 
in favour of the management. The Tribunal can- 
not sit in appeal over the findings of the Enquiry 
Officer and can only interfere with the step taken 
by the management against the delinquent worker 
on the basis of the findings at the enquiry only 
if the enquiry has vitiated against the principles 
of natural justice or the findings of the Enquiry 
Officer was perverse or the action taken by the 
management was taken only by way of victimisa- 
tion, und amounted to unfatr labour practice. In 
the instant case (le main complaint of the workers 
was that in the enquiry they were not given all 
reasonable opportunities to defend  thomselves. 
The allegation of the workers has been seriously 
challenged by the company and it has examined 
115 Enquiry Officer and also produced the proceed- 
ings of the enquiry to refute these allegations. 
The proceedings of the enquiry with the findings 
of the Enquiry Officer is Ext, B in the ense. Pages 
1 to 32 of this Exhibit was the Enquiry Officer's 
report and findings regarding the enquiry and the 
rest of the document contain the charge-sheets, 
workers’ reply thereto, evidence recorded at the 
enquiry and some other documents. The Enquiry 
Officer's report was prefaced with an introdvetion 
and in the said introduction is given a time table 
said to have been observed by the Enquiry Officer 
in the enquiries. The time table indicates thui 
the enquiry had commenced on and from 28th June 
1963, and it is not disputed that the workers were 
duly notified that the enquiry would commence 
from 28th June L963. It 1a also not disputed that 
at the said enquiry the workers were represented 
hy Shri A. K. Sinha. According to the time table 
the only work done on 28th June 1963 was the exa- 
mination and cross-examination of two witnesses for 
the company but if we go through the proceedings of 
that date it will appear that the examination of the 
two concerned workers, and from the manner in 
which their statements of that date were recorded 
by the Enquiry Officer, it can be said without any 
hesitation that these statements were made by the 
two workers in answer to questions put by the En- 
quiry Officer and not suo moto. In a departmental 
enquiry company must begin first i.e. its witnesses 
must first be examined and cross-examined and 
then the witnesses for the defence including the 


concerned workers. Examination of the two 


workers on 29th June 1963 by the Enquiry Officer 


not appear before him but for his non-appearance 
no adverse presumption can be drawn against him, 
us his appearance on that date was insisted on by 
the enquiry officer for clarification of certain facts 
und not for his evidence in support of his case. The 
procedure followed by the enquiry officer to take 
evidence in the enquiry, was for all these reasons, 
was irregular and improper, and for this reason 
alone it can be held that the enquiry was not fair 
and proper. 


_ The procedure followed at the enquiry was also 
irregular and improper in as much as the enquiry 
officer had allowed the company to lead evidence 
after close of defence evidence, obviously with 
the idea to nullify the effects of the evidence 
ndduced on behalf of the workers. Shri A. K.

pay in lieu of notice. 


In view of the findings and discussions above 
made, an award dismissing the union’s prayer for 
declaration that the dismissal of Shri Sarkar was 
unjustified and illegal, and directing the com- 
pany to pay Shri Mukherji compensation at the 
rate of one month’s pay for each year of his com- 
pleted service under it plus one month’s pay in 
lieu of notice, is passed. 


The award so far it relates to Shri Mukhenji is 


to be implemented within a month from the date 


of publication in the ‘‘Calcutta Gazette’’. 
This is my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me.

the first portion of Charge No. 3 if not on any other

1 have already commented that this charge was 
extremely vague and cannot, therefore, be 
sustained, 


The 6th charge of Shri Sarkar was that he had 
taken Rs, 2 from Shri A. K. Roy for purchasing 
engine oil but he did not purchase the same there- 
by running the risk of damaging the engine of 
the vehicle. It bas already been held that Shri 
A. .کا‎ Roy was the last officer to be dropped by 
Shri Sarkar that night and it is not disputed that 
while dropping Shri Roy he had taken from him 
Rs. 2 for purchase of engine oil. In his evidence 
before this Tribunal Shri Sarkar stated that after 
leaving the 15105010015) Place he had purchased en- 
gine oil from a garage at Gariahat Road. Corro- 
boration to this statement of Shri Sarkar is avail- 
able from the evidence of Shri Mukherji but no 
evidence contradicting ‘this case of Shri Sarkar 
wus adduced by the company, It is not therefore 
possible for me to find him guilty of this charge.

excepting the first portion of charge No. 9, none 
of the other charges agu.nst Shni Sarkar has been 
established by the evidence led by the company 
before this Tribunal. - The first portion of charge 
No. 3 was, however, in the opinion of this Tribu- 
nal, sufficient for dismissal of Shri Sarkar. It 
must accordingly be held that the dismissal of 
Shri Sarkar was justified and legal. It was no 
doubt argued on behalf of Shni Sarkar that when 
there were several charges against Shri Sarkar and 
most of them have fmled, this Tribunal should 
not uphold his dismissal, but this argument on 
behaif ‘of Shri Sarkar, 1 cannot uphold when I am 
sutisfied beyond all doubts that on the material. 
night Shri Sarkar was guilty of gross negligence 
of duty, for not taking adequate precaution agaiust 
the damage of company’s vehicle after it had 
caught fire, 


Against Shri Mukherji there are as many as 
three charges. In view of the discussions already 
made, :) must he held that none of these charges 
has been substantiated. He was in the car.with 
the permission of Shri Garkar and the duty to 
take care of the car was with Shri Sarkar. If, 
therefore, he had left the place after the arrival 
of the Fire Brigade or the Police Officer without 
arranging for the safety of the car, he has there- 
fore committed any offence sufficient for his dis- 
missal. His dismissal on the charges brought 
against him, was in these circumstances unjusti- 
fied and illegal. But though J am satisfied that 
the company was not justified to dismiss him for 
the reasons stated in the charge-sheet issued to 
him, I cannot ask the company to reinstate him 
and:I hold that proper justice would be done to 
him and if the Company instead of reinstatement 
he is given compensation in accordance with law.

has stated that on 3rd January 1966 Sarju Mondal

ant would not be coming back to do work. Qn con- 
sidering the evidence of witnesses and circumstances, 
J hold that the story ৪০৮ up by the union that Sarju 
Mandal had been dismissed by the company is not 
true. In fact, Sarju Mandal voluntarily 10 the service 
of the'company on 3rd January 1966 after taking all 
his dues. I also find that the story of victimisation 
or malice on the part of the company is not correct. 
The evidence of Sarju Mondal is unreliable and uncorro- 
borated. The present case appears to be a speculative 
one. As Sarju Mandal has given up his service volun- 
tarily, he can get no relief. 


In the order of reference it has been stated that it is 
a dispute between the company and its workmen. 
There is no evidence on the side of the union that there 
was ever any dispute between the company and any 
other workman. The company deals in biri leaves 
and the union described as representing the workmen 
of the company is an organisation of motor drivers. 
There is no evidence also that except Sarju Mandal 
any other workman of the company was a menrber 
of the union. I find no evidence to prove that the 
union had any authority to represent the workmen of 
the company in the present reference. ' 


In view of my findings above, I decide the issue 
against Sarju Mandal and I find that he is ontitled to 
no relief in this case.

Mitra is justified? What reliof, if any, is he 
entitled to ? 


On receipt of the order of reference usual notices 
were issucd to the parties fixing 26th May 1966 for their 
appearance as also for the filing of the written statement 
by the Union. Notices were duly served and the Union 
appeared and filed its written statoment. In the written 
statement filed on behalf of the Union it has been stated 
that the concerned worker Shri Dipen Kumar Mitra 
was under the employment of Shri N.K.Mukherji and 
Shri N.C. Mukherji, as a cleaner in their Bus No.WBR 
1041 in route No. 85 from Barrackpore to Kanchrapara 
1)২: wee summarily cismigsed from service by the pro- 
prie‘ors of the Eus co l0th 8187 1965. Over the dis- 
mixsal the Union 11১৪৫) an incustiinl dispute unc tle 
case was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication of the 
issue set forth above. 


Though notices of the reference case were duly 
served on the Mukherjis, none of them appeared to 
justify the dismissal of the concerned worker. Accord- 
ingly the case was taken up for hearing on 4th April 1967. 
On that date the Union examined the concerned worker 
Shri Dipen Kumar Mitra and in hig evidence 
before this Tribunal, he has said that he was a cleaner 
in Bus No. WBR 1041 belonging to the Mukherjis, 
for about threo years and that on 10th May 1965, his 
employers had verbally terminated his service without 
assigning any reason whatsoever. This evidence of 
Shri Mitra, which I find no reason to disbelieve, 
conclusively establishes that the owners of the Bus 
have dismissed him from service without any charge 
and without even giving him any hearing. Dis- 
missal of Shri Mitra was in the ciroumstances, quite 
illegal and unjustified. 86 is accordingly entitled 
to reinstatement with all wages and other allowances, 
if any, since his dismissal. 

In view of the findings aforesaid, an award directing 
Messrs. N.K.Mukheji and N.C. Mukherji to reinstate 
the concerned worker Shri Dipen Kumar Mitra with all 
wages and other allowances, if any, during the period of 
his forced unemployment is passed. 


This is my award. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 
S.K. DATTA GUPTA, Judge.

NOVEMBER 1967 


THE Union Public Service Commission will hold an 
examination at Ahmedabad, Allahabad, Bangalore, Bhupal, 
Bombay, Calcutta, Cuttack, Dclhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Jammu, 
Madras, Nagpur, Patiala, Patna, Shillong and Trivandrum 
on 9th and 10th November 1967 for entry into the Indian 
Military Academy. Age-limits: Candidates must have been 
born not earlier than 2nd July 1947 and not later than 
Ist July 1950. These age-limits can in no case be relaxed. 
Qualifications: Intermediate or equivalent. Applications 
from candidates who have appeared or intend to appear at 
Intermediate or cquivalent examination acceptable provi- 
sionally. Full particulars and application forms obtainable 
from Secretary, Union Public Service Commission, Dholpur 
Hqause. New Delhi-11, by remitting Re. 1.00 by money order

Omice. (This amount is neither refundable . ہ٥‎ adjustable 
towards fee). Candidates must clearly state on money 
order coupons “INDIAN MILITARY ACADEMY EXAMI- 
NATION, NOVEMBER 1967" and also give their names 
and full postal addresses in block letters. . Postal orders 
or cheques or currency notes not acceptable in lieu of money 
orders. Full particulars and application forms also obtain- 
able free from nearest Recruiting Office, Military AreajSub- 
Area Headquarters or National 09681 Corps Unit. Only 
Unmarried male candidates eligible for admission to the 
Examination. Completed applications must reach Union 
Public Service Commission by 28th June 1967 (10th July 
1967 for candidates residing abroad and in Andaman aod

Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (III of 1897), the Governor is pleased to prescribe 
the following temporary regulations for the prevention and control of smali-pox 
and for the medical inspection, isolation, observation and surveillance of persons 
suffering from, or suspected of being infected with, small-pox in the said 
district for a period of six months:— 


TEMPORARY REGULATIONS FOR THE PREVENTION AND CONTROL 
OF SMALL-POX 


1. In these regulations unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or 
context.— 


(a) “Health Officer” means the Health Officer of the district appointed 
by the State Government, the Chief Medical Officer of Health of the 
district, or the Subdivisional Health Officer of any of the snb- 
divisions of the district within their respective subdivisions; 


(b) “Sanitary Inspector” means a Sanitary Inspector appointed by the 
State Government; 


(6) “Small-pox” means any disease accompanied by an eruption of v. eich £ 
or pustules;

(d) “Patient” means a person suffering from or suspected to be suffering 
from small-pox; 


(e) “Medical practitioner” means any person practising the medical 
profession, 


Notices 


2. If in any case the Health Officer considers that the issue of a notice 
under these rcgulations is likely to lead to such an amount of delay as might 
facilitate the spread of small-pox he may forthwith take such steps as he may 
think fit for carrying out the work, and shall thereafter, as soon as possible, 


issuc a notice on the person concerned stating the reasons why such work has 
been carried out. 


3. If any measure which the Health Officer has by a notice issued under 
these regulations, required to be carried out, be not carried out to his satisfac- 


tion within the time stated in the notice the Health Officer shall be entitled to 
carry out the measure. 


Costs and compensation 


4. (1) All expenses incurred in carrying out any work in pursuance of 
an order issued under these regulations shall be paid by the State Government 
except in any case where the order directs a person to carry out any work in 


relation to property in his possession, in which case the expenses shall be paid’ 


by such person: 


Provided that where the conditions which led the Health Officer to pass 
such an order, are not attributable to any act or default of the person in 
possession of the property, the State Government may pay to such person the 
whole or a part of the expenses incurred by him in carrying out the order. 


(2) The State Government may recover all expenses incurred by the Health 
Officer in carrying out the measure under regulation 3 from the person or 
persons to whom the notice was originally issued. 


5. The State Government shall pay adequate compensation to any person 
who has sustained substantial loss or damage by reason of anything done under 
these regulations: 


Provided that no person shall receive any compensation for anything done 
or suffered under these regulations if he has failed to carry out an order issued 
under these regulations. He shall not direct the patient to be removed from 
the house unless it is, in his opinion, impossible to make proper arrangements 
for his isolation therein within the time specified in the order and to the 
satisfaction of the Health Officer. 


Location of disease 


6. When a case of small-pox occurs in a house, the nearest male relative 
in attendance upon the patient, or in the absence of any such relative the 
occupier of the house, or if the occupier be the patient, the senior male inmate 
of the house other than the patient of the house shall, within twenty-four hours 
of the onset of the disease, give information regarding the -occurrence of such 
case either personally or in writing or by means of the chaukidar or other 
village watchmen or headman to the nearest Sanitary Inspector.

7. (1) Every medical practitioner called in to attend upon any case of 
amall-pox shall forthwith vive notice of the ease by a special messenger to 
the nearest Sanitary Inspector or to the Health Officer by post and the cost 
of such messenger in each cuse shall be defrayed by the State Government. 


2) The doctor-in-charge of a hospital or a dispensary within the district 
shall forthwith give notice of any case of small-pox brought to such hospital 
or dispensary for treatment to the nearest Sanitary Inspector by a special 
messenger and to the Health Officer by post, and the cost in each case shall 
be defrayed by the State Government. 


8. Thana officers shall supply to the Health Officer such periodical returns 
of cases of small-pox as he may from time to time call upon them to furnish. 


9, The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may examine any person 
who is, or suspected to be, suffering from small-pox or who, in his opinion, 
may be infected with or likely to spread small-pox. 


Isolation of patients 


10. When the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers that the 
isolation of any patient is a precaution necessary for the protection of the 
neighbouring population, he shall order the patient to observe isolation and 
may order the nearest relative in attendance on the patient, or the occupier 
of the house in which the paticnt is staying, to arrange for the isolation of 
the patient in such a manner and for such a time as may be approved by the 
Health Officer. 


11. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that any person, 
who has been in contact with a person found to be suffering from small-pox, 
shall be segregated for a period not exceeding a fortnight In a manner and in 
a place to be approved by the Health Officcr. 


- 12. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that any person 
who has been in contact with a person found to be suffering from small-pox 
shall be vaccinated or re-vaccinated within a time to be specified in the order. 


13. No person shall enter any place wherein a patient its isolated under 
regulation 10, without the permission of the Health Officer or a Sanitary 
Inspector. 


14. When a patient has been removed from a house for isolation under 
regulation 10, the State Government shall provide for him free of charge a 
suitable place, with necessary attendants, diet, etc. 


15. No person, who is or has been suffering from small-pox, shall leave 
the place where he has been staying until he has received from the Health 


Officer or a Sanitary Inspector written permission to do so. 


16. No person while suffering from evident symptoms of small-pox or in 
the convalescent state of the disease with scabs of pocks on his body shall 
expose himself in any street, road, public place, shop, bazar or any place used 
in common by persons other than members of the family or household to which 
such infected person belongs or shall move from place to place unless he is 
proceeding to a hospital for admission and treatment.

17. The Health Officer or u Sanitary Inspector authorised by the Health 
Officer in writing in that behalf may, during the prevalence of any outbreak © 
of small-pox, order that any bazar, shop or other public place shall remain 
closed for such time as may appear to him to be necessary and may forbid the 
holding of any fair, mela, or other gathering to which people from several 
villages commonly or periodically resort. 


Miscellancous 


18. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may require any person to 
allow to be carried out by such agency and within such time as may be specified 
in the order, such measures for the disinfection of any premises in the occupation 
of such person or for the disinfection or destruction of any of his personal 
effects, as the said officer or inspector may consider necessary. 


19. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may direct the owner or 
occupier of any premises to take steps to have vaccinated or re-vaccinated within 
a time to be specified in the order any person residing on such premises and 
under the control of such owner or occupier if the Health Officer is of opinion 
that such person has been in contact with any one suffering from small-pox. 


2). The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may forbid any person who 
has been a patient or who has to his knowledge bcen in contact with a patient 
to act as vendor of any article for such pcriod as may be specified in the 
order. 


21. No person shall sell any article which has been in contact with a 
patient until it has been disinfected to the satisfaction of the Health Officer 
or a Sanitary Inspector. 


22. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may issue general orders 
that by a specified date certain sanitary precautions of a simple nature, such 
as lime-washing of houses, clearing of latrines or the removal of filth or rubbish 
shall be carried out to his satisfaction. 


23. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may prohibit persons from 
retaining or selling cloths taken from the bodies of persons who have died of 
small-pox and may cause any such clothes to be destroyed. 


24. No person shall carry or permit to be carried in a public conveyance 
w patient except in the case where a patient is carried to a hospital with the 
following precautions against spreading the disease, namely:— 


(i) that he is so well covered that the discharge and scabs from the 
lesions do not come directly into touch with the body of the 
conveyance; 


(ii) that he is taken to the hospital direct and the conveyance does not 
halt at any other place for transacting any business; and 


(iii) that excepting one or two attendants for the patient no other person 
is carried in the conveyance at the same time.

of formalin (1 in 400), lysol (1 in 500), izol (1 in 500), or of

such station; and 


(iii) in the case of a conveyance carrying a dead body to the burial or 
cremation ground, by the owner of the conveyance himself and 
such owner shall effect the disinfection with a strong solution of

from the lesions do not come directly into touch with the body 
of the conveyance;

28. No person shall, without the written permission of the Health Officer. : 
dispose of any corpse except by burning or burial. ০০ 


29. The Health Officer may approve burning or burial grounds and may 
by order direct either generally or specially in respect to any specified area, 
that corpses shall not be burned or buried at places other than those so 
approved by him. 


30. Any person burning or Pope to be burnt any corpse shall cause 
the same to be completely reduced to ashes and shall likewise cause the clothes 
or other articles brought with such corpse to be reduced to ashes. 


31. The Health Officer may direct that no person shall bury or cause to 
be buried any corpse, which, in the opinion of the Health Officer, is likely 
to spread small-pox, in a grave, not constructed of masonry and less than 
6 feet deep. 


32. The Health Officer may order that no dome or other person employed 
for the disposal of corpses shall withdraw from his duties without the permission 
of the Health Officer unless such dome or other person has given notice in 
writing not less than one month previously of his intention so to withdraw. 


33. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may themselves or through 
any person authorised by the Health Officer or the Sanitary Inspector in that 
behalf seize and dispose of any corpse which in the opinion of the said officer 
or inspector is infected with or is likely to spread small-pox, unless the relatives 
or friends of the deceased person satisfy him that they are prepared and able 
to dispose of the corpse in a manner which will prevent the spread of small- 


pox. 


34. (1) The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may require any 
person who appears to be acquainted with facts in connection with any case 
or suspected case of small-pox to attend before him at a time to be stated 
in the order and at any .place not more than one mile from the place where 
such person resides or is staying when the order is issued, and such person 
shall appear as so required. 


(2) When the person summoned to appear under paragraph (1) is a female 
who, by the custom of the country, docs not appear in public, suitable precaution 
shall be taken to respect the said custom. 


35. (1) The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may examine orally 
any person who appears to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of 
a case or suspected case of small-pox. 


(2) When the person to be examined under paragraph (1) is a female 
who, by the custom of the country, does not سا‎ pe in public the officer shall 
take her atatement under such conditions as shall admit of due respect of the 
said custom. 


(3) Such person shall be bound to answer questions relating to such case 
put to him or her by such officer, other than questions the answers to which 
would have a tendency to expose him or her to any criminal charge. 


36. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may, with such assistants 
(if any) as he thinks fit, enter upon any land, or after two hours’ notice in 
writing, into any premises or building used for human habitation at any time 
between sunrise and sunset for the purpose of carrying out any measure or 
making any enquiries authorised by these regulations.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF FOOD AND SUPPLIES 


ORDERS 

No. 3480-F.S. / FS / 14-94 /67.—19th May 1967.—Whereas the Governor 
is of opinion that it is necessary and expedient so to do for maintaining 
supplies of foodgrains and securing their equitable distribution and 
availability at fatr prices in the State of West Bengal; 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the 
Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (Act 10 of 1955) and, in particular, by না) 
section (3B) thereof, read with the Government of India, Ministry of Food, 
Agriculture, Community Development and Co-operation (Department of 
Food), order No. G@.S.R. 906, dated the Yth June 1966, as subsequently 
amended, the Governor is pleased hereby to make, with the prior concurrence 
of the Central Government, the following Order, namely :— 


1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(1) This Order may be 
called the West Benga) Foodgrains (Requisitioning) Order, 1967. 


(2) It extends to the whole of West Bengal. 
(3) This Order shall come into force at once. 


2. Doefinitions.—In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires,-— 

(a) ‘consumer’? means uw person who purchases foodgrains for con- 

sumption by himself and the members of his family and includes 

an institution or establishment which purchases foodgrains for 
consumption by its members and staff; 

(b) ‘family’? includes servants living in the same mess and, in the 
case of an institution or estublishment, all its members and 
ataff ; 

(c) ‘‘foudgrains’’? means rice or paddy; 

(l) “institution” and “establishment”? have the same meanmgs as in 
the West Rengal Rationing Order, 1964; 

(৮) “procurement agent’? means a person who has entered into an 
agreenient with the State Government for purchase, sale or 
storage of foodgrains on behalf of the State Government and 
includes the Food Corporation of India, established under the 
Food Corporations Act, 1964 (37 of 1964), acting as an agent 
of the State Government for the purposes of this Order;

3. Power of the requiring authority to call for accounts and information. 
—-Every persou holding in stock any foédgrains shall, whon called upon 
to do so by the requiring authority by an ordor in writing, furnish— 


(a) a true account of such foodgrains, and 


(b) information regarding the production, storage, acquisition, use 
or consumption of such foodgrains in such manner and within 
such period us may be specified in the order and a person whea 
so called upon’ shall not, unless permitted by the requiring 
authority, sell or otherwise dispose of such foodgrains or any 
part thereof. 


4. Power of the requiring authority to direct sale.—(1) Subject to 
the provisions of sub-paragraph (3), the requiring authority may, by an 
order in writing, direct any person holding in stock any foodgrains to sell 
at the procurement price such quantity of such foodgrains to such person 
or such procurement agent or such officer of the State Government and 
within such period as may he specified in the order. 


(2) Every such order shall specify the following particulars, nomely :— 


(a) the quantity and variety or grade of foodgrains held in stock by 
such person ; 


(b) the quantity in respect of which exemption is granted to such 
person under the provisions of sub-paragraph (3) ; 


(c) the quantity and variety or grade of foodgrains required to be sold 
by such person; and 


(0) the place at which and the period within which the foodgraing 
directed ا١‎ be sold by such person are to be delivered. 


(3) A producer or consumer mentioned in column 1 of the Table below 
shall, for all or any of the purposes mentioned in column 2 of the Table, 
he entitled to hold in stock the quantity of foodgrains caleulated according 
to the seale mentioned in the corresponding eniries in column 8 or column

(3) ‘'Mine’? and ‘‘Superfine’’, in relation to grade of aman paddy and

eolumns 2 and 0 of Schedule TIL and inelude similar grades. 


6. Disposal of disputes.—(1) Any person who has been directed by an 
‘order under sub-paragraph 01) of paragraph 4 to sell the foodgrains held 
in stock by him may, before the expiry of the period mentioned in such 
order, apply in writing to the requiring authority disputing the correctness 
or accuracy of such order in respect of any material fact or detail. 


— (2) The requiring authority shall, on receiving the application, forth- 
with forward it to the District Officer having jurisdiction in the area where 
the stock ٠× held by such person. 


(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-paragraph (1) of 
paragraph 4, it shall be lawful for such person to hold.in stock the food- 
grains m respect of: which the dispute has arisen till a decision is given 
by the District Officer : | 


Provided that where the dispute relutes to the quantity of foodgrains 
{o he exempted from. selling and such person claims that he is entitled to 
more than what has been exempted, he shall, before making an application 
under sub-paragraph (1), sell the stock, if any, in excess of what has been 
claimed by him. 


(4) The I)istrict Officer, ou receiving an application forwarded to him 
by the requiring, authority under sub-paragraph (2). shall after giving the 
applicant an opportunity of beimg heard and after taking such evidence us 
he deen necessary, dispose of the application as expeditiously as possible. 
The decision of the District Officer shall he binding on the applicant and 
the requiring authority. 


(5) 1f a dispute falls within the proyiso to sub-paragraph (3), the. 
District Officer shall not entertain the application, uuless he is satisfied 
that the applicant has complied with the provisions of the said proviso, 


(6) 11 the District Officer decides that the applicant is lable to sell 
the whole of {Ke stock specified in the order made under sub-paragraph (1) 
of paragraph 4, or any part thereof, the District Officer shal] direct the 
applicant 10 sell such stock to sueh person or such officer of the State 
Government and within such period as may be specified in the decision. 


Explanation.—(1) For the purposes of this paragraph ‘‘Diatrict Officer” 
means, in relation to a district, the District Magistrate or the Deputy 
Conmmissioner of that district, and, in relation to Calcutta Area, the Director 
Commissioner of that district, and in relntion to Calcutta Area, the Director 
of Rationing, West Bengal. 


(2) “Calcutta Area’? means the areas described m Schedule I to the 
‘alcutta Municipal Act, 1951 (West. Bengal Act XXXIITI of 1951), as 
amended by notification issued under section 594 of that Act; that part 
of Hastings north of south edge of Clyde Row and Strand Road to the 
river bank and the area within the limits of the Port of Calcutta as defined 
by notification under section 5 of the Indian Port Act, 1908 (XV of 1908).

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the 
Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1965), read with the Government 
of Indin, Ministry of Food, Agriculture, Community Development and 
Co-operation (Department of Food), Order No. G.S.R. 906, dated the 9th 
June 1966, as subsequently amended, the Governor is ylens:d herzby to 
make the following order, namely سے‎ 


1, Short title, extent and commencement. -(1) This order may he 
oth 875 Bengal Rice and Paddy (Storage by Consumers) Control 
rder, 1901. 


(2) It extends to the whole of West Mengal except the areas in which 
the West Bengal Rationing Order, 1964, is in force. 


(3) It shall come into force on and from the 20th May 1967. 
2. Definitions.—In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) “consumer’’ means a person who purchases rice or paddy for 
consumption by himself and the members of his family and his 
servants living in the same mess with him, but does not include 
an establishment or an institution or a producer; 


Explanation.—For the purposes of this clause,— 


(1) al] consumers living in the same mess shall be treated as a 
single consumer; 


(ii) ‘establishment’? und ‘‘institution’’ shall have the same 
meanings as in the West Bengal Rationing Order, 1964. 


(b) ‘paddy equivalent’? in respect of any quantity of rice means a 
quantity of paddy equal to one and a half times the quantity of 
rice ; 

(c) ‘‘producer’’ means « person who grows paddy or causes paddy to 
be grown on any land in West Bengal; 


(1) “riee’” includes broken rice, but does not include chira, muri or 
hot, 


3. Limitation on storage of rice or paddy.—(1) No consumer = shall 
store or have in his possession at any one time,— 


(a) more than 2.6 quintale of rice, or 
(b) more than 3.9 quintals of paddy, or 


(c) where a consumer stores or has in his possession both rice and 
paddy, more than 3.9 quintals of paddy and paddy equivalent of 
rice in the aggregate. 


(2) Sub-puragraph (1) shall also apply in’ the case of a producer i 
respect of any rice or paddy stored or held in possession by him other than 
the paddy grown or caused to be grown by him and the rice made 


therefrom. 


4. Effect on the West Bengal Rice and Paddy (Declaration of Stocks 
and Licensing) Order, 1967.—This Order shall have effect notwithstanding 
anything contained in the West Bengal Rice and Paddy ) Declaration of 
Stocks and Ticensing) Order, 1967. 


5. Powers of entry, search, seizure, etc.—(1) Any officer in the 
Department of Food and Supplies not below the rank of Sub-Inspector or 
any Police Officer not below the rank of Assistant Sub-Inspector or any 
(Mficer under the Regional Director (Food), Eastern Region, Ministry of 
Food, Agrioulture,.Community Development and Co-operation, (Department 
of Food), Government of India, not below the rank of Inspector, may,

with a view to securing compliance with this Order or to satisfying himself 
that this Order has heen complied with,— 


(a) inspect or cause to be inspected any book or documents or accounts 
as well as any stocks of rice or paddy belonging to or under 1109 
control of any person, 

(b) require any person to give any information in bis possession with 
respect to purchase, sale or storage of rice or paddy, 

(c) stop and search forthwith, with such aid or assistance as may 19

(৮) ৪6148 and remove, with such aid or assistance as may be necessury,

and the animals, vehicles, vessels or other conveyances used in 
carrying such stocks, if he has reason to suspect that any 
provision of this Order has been, is being, or is about to be,

reapect of any other stock of rice or paddy, which, immediately 
before the contravention, was stored or possessed along with 
such stocks and thereafter take or authorise the taking of all

(10 of 1955), and for their safe custody pending such production: | 


Provided that in exercising the powers under this sub-paragraph cue 
regard shall be paid to the social and religious customs of the

(2) The provisions of sections 102 and 103 of the Code of Crimmal

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


CaLcuTra, 


Amend- 
ment of 
section 139. 


Ameond- 
ment of 
section 142, 


Apart from amendments relating to conversions to metric measures and 
decimal coinage, the Bill seeks to provide for service of notice on and the 
right to make representations by the owners of lands in non-municipal areas, 
just as in the case of the owners of lands in municipal areas; and it further 
provides for a review of the plan of a public street or a public park where 
the project is not accomplished within ten years so that in suitable cases 
the lands concerned may be released from restrictions regarding their use.

No. 3605Ac.—I1th May 1967.—In exercise of the 
powers vested in me under Article 229(2) of the 
Constitution of India, I do hereby make the follow- 
ing rules with the approval of the Governor: — 


Rules 


1. These rules shall be called the High Court 
Services (Revision of Pension) Rules, 1966. 


They shall be deemed to have come into force 
on the 7th June 1966. 


2. Rules 2 to 10 of the West Bengal Services 
(Revision of Pension) Rules, 1966, as promulgated 
with Finance Department Notification No. 2799-7 
FIP-28/65, dated the 16th July 1966, shall apply 
mutatis mutandis to all persons under the employ- 
ment of the High Court, who hold a lien on a 
পি pensionable post or would have held a 
ien on such a post had their lien not been 
suspended: 


Provided that all persons who were in permanent 
and pensionable service of the High Court ×ہ‎ the 
7th June 1966 shall have the option to remain on 
the existing rules. Where the option to remain on 
the existing rules is exercised, it shall be communi- 
cated in writing to the Head of the Office in the 
case of a non-gazetted officer and to the Accountant- 
General, West Bengal, in the case of a gazetted ° 
officer of the High Court within a period of one year 
from the date of notification of these rules in the 
“Calcutta Gazette” or the actual date of retirement, 
whichever is earlicr. The option once exercised 
shall be final and cannot be modified at any sub- 
sequent date: 


Provided further that the expression “existing 
rules” appearing in the said rules shall, in the case 
of persons under the employment of the High Court, 
mean the corresponding rules applicable to them 
including the provisions in the pension rules in the 
Civil Service Regulations. 


3. These rules shall not apply to the holder of 
any of the posts under the High Court, who is a 
niember of the West Bengal Higher Judicial Service. 

D. N. SINHA, 


Chief Justice.

the case of G. C. Industries Mazdoor Union reperted in 
1962, L. A. 0. page 178 it was pointed out by the Labour 
Appellate Tribunal] that scales or yrades of pay should 
not be forced upon an employer of industrial labour 01৯ 
less it was established that the employer have to the pre- 
sent capacty to pay and the financial capacity can be 
counted on in future. [t was pointed out therein that

of wages, even it, it was shown that the industry has 
been able to make substantial profit in a particular

units cither in the region or elsewhere and the industry- 
cum-region formula innunciated by the Supreme Court 
in the Express Newspapers (P) Ltds. (1961, 1, L. L. শ. 
page 339) and other cases cannot be said to be applicable 
in the instant case. The Labour Appellate Tribun::! in 
the Caltex caso بر‎ কা in 1962 .ہا‎ A. 0. page 402 
observed that to determine fair wage the important 
factor was the capacity of the industry to pay and 
the prevailing rate of wages which was not to be 
appraised on the footing of industry-cum régions basis. 


Question now for decision is what would be the 
basis in dotermining the grades and scales of pay fer 
the workers in a concern for which there are no compara- 
ble units. There are certain widely accepted princi- 
ples which has got to be scrutinised before framing 
& wage structure for any industry. These principles 
are to be found in the report of the Fair Wage Commi- 
ttee. The floor level of wages as formulated by the 
Fair Wage Committee and as observe! by the Suprome 
Court in a number of decisions does not depend upon 
the capacity of the industry to pay but the upper 
limit of the wages is restricted by what is called tho 
capacity of the industry to pay. This capacity is not 
the capacity of a particular unit but capacity of the 
entire industry on an indystry-cum-region basis. The 
Fair Wage Committee took four factors into considera- 
tion in determining the level of fair wages. They are: 


(a) prevailing ratos of wages in the same or similar 
occupation in 6119: same or neighbonring 
localities ; 


(b) productivity of labour ; 


(c) level of National income and its distribution ; 
and 


(d) place of industry in the economy of the country. 


The Labour Appellate Tribunal (1952 L. A. C. 490) 
did not attach much importance of the productivity 
of the labour and place of industry factor but they 
attached great importance in the prevailing rate of 
wages in the same or similar occupation in the 
same region as it was capable of more pricise definition 
than other factors. Unless level of wages of workers 
employed in similar occupation in the neighbourhood 
was Maintained, thore was likelyhood of an over 
flow of labuur because of better level of Wages from one 
industry to another but there was also the question of 
industrial unrest, should the wage for one industry 
be fixed without regard to the prevailing rates of wages 
in similar industries in the neighbourho@&. So tho 
Tribunal should havo regard to the current condition

Issue No. ও 
Dearness allowance 


The Union claimed dearness allowance at tho rate 
of 50 per cent. of the basic pay with a minimum of 
Rs. 35. In demanding the cearness allowance the Union 
contends that this is the minimum which should cover 
the bare minimum needs of the workers and is just 
sufficient to keep them above starvation. The question 
of financial capacity should not come into play in paying 
this minimum. The company, on the other hand 
contends that it pays 25 per cent. of the basic pay to 
‘the workmen as cearncss allowance and characterised 
the claim of the Union as fantastic. 


The wages fixed for the workers cannot be regarded 
even as fair wages in the content of present day price 
index having regarée. to the minimum rate of wages for 
the oil mill workers of West Bengal, discussec above, 
present day rate of dearness allowance for the workers 
in this concern clearly appear to be inadequate and 
unsatisfactory. Undoubtedly there has heen a rise 
in the living index as reflected in the consumer price 
index number for the working class in Calcutta. The 
average cost of living index for the year 1965 was 507 
and that for 1966 would be above 550. THe present 
rate of dearness allowance of the company is not cal. 
culated upon any scientific basis and the cost of living 
index has not been taken into consideration in the matter 
of fixation of the dearness allowance. That being the 
position and as the workers are going to get a pay riso 
not more than اا5‎ per cent. neutralisation should be 
allowed. Third Major Engineering Tribunal fixed the 
dearness allowance for the working class on a aliding

AWARD 


The Government of Wost Bengal, in the Dopartment 
of Labour, by order No. 1249-1.R./IR/11L-19/65, dated 
the 28th March 1966, has referred under section 10 of 
the Industrial Dieputer Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
existing between Mesere. ‘Imperial Roller Flour Mills 
Ltd., 243/A Manicktolla Main Road, Calcutta, and 
their workmen represented by West Bengal Flour Mills 
Mazdoor Congress, 109/Z Ultadanga Main Road, 
Calcutta-4, to this Tribunal for adjudication on the 
issue mentoned in the order of reference and 
reproduced below :— 


(1) Whether the workmen are entitled to any 
compensation and/or relief in addition to what 
has been paid to them by way of compensation 
for the lay-off for the period from 12th November 
1964 to llth January 1965?

van'No. WRV 820 for carrying the goods of the com- 
jpany with Salesman Shri Achinta Kumar Das Gupta 
when asked by Store in-charge Sachin Ghosh at about 
10 a.m. on 1061) February 1965. From the evidence 
it is clear that Gopiram was disinclined to drive the 
van for various reasons. First he stated that the van 
was out of order. When the service of the mechanic 
had been requisitioned and it became known that the 
van had been set right in the previous cvening and it 
was pointed out to him, Gopiram allegedly left the 
ven with the keys with him. Secondly, he said that 
his duty period was up to 2 p.m. and the assignment was 
not likely to be completed by that time. He was 
unwilling to go out and lastly he gave out that he was 
feeling sick and he wanted to be relieved carlier. Several 
witnesses have proved this fact and the inference is 
irresistable that Gopiram was unwilling to perform his 
duty on pretexts, none of which appear to be convincing. 
The enquiring officer gave out claborate reasons for 
his conclusion and none of the witnesses appear to be 
biased or prejudiced against Gopiram. In fact some 
wanted to justify his action. The enquiry was done in 
& proper and fair manner and Gopiram himself admitted 
that. Principle of natural justice was in no way 
violated and on a careful consideration of all the 
materials on record I do not see any reason to differ 
from the finding of tho enquiring officer in so far as 
charge No. 1 is concerned. That being a major misdame 
anour within the meaning of paragraph 14(b)(i) of the 
Model Standing Orders which in the absence of the 
Standing of its own, will be regarded as standing orders 
of the company undcr section 12A of the Industrial 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, the manage- 
ment cannot be said to be unjustified in taking action 
against Gopiram and the cismissa] in the instant case 
ae be held justified and he is not entitled to any 
relief. 


As for Gopi Chandra Dey, it is to be pointed out that 
the Union did not sponsore his 0980 any longer as ho 
wanted to dissociate himaclf with this adjudication. 
He filed an application to the Tribunal on 1st December 
1966 inter alia stating that he was no longer a member 
of the Union and did not want to porsue the case and 
also informed the Union about this fact. Gopal Dey 
was present on that day and his identification was not 
disputed on behalf of the Union. That being the 
position and as the case was not pressed by the 
union, justify the issue regarding dismissal of Gopal 
Chandra Dey is hereby dropped. 


This is the award of the Tribunal.

the Ist July 1967.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. The India Jute Company Ltd. (Cotton 
Mill Section), P.O. Serampore, district Hooghly 
(Registered Office at 16 Strand Road, 
Calcutta-1), and their workmen represented by 
(1) Serampore Subdivisional Cotton Textile 


(Part IC 


1654 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, MAY 27, 1967 


than what they used to earn when  time-rate ray- 
ment was prevalent. The Company also compen- 
sated the workmen for their average loss in earnings,’ 
though the workmen failed to give normal produc- 
lion because of their low efficiency. No notice 
under section 9A of the Industrial Disputes Act is 
required to be given in the present case. It has 
further been alleged by the Company that cnly 24 
workmen have been affected by the introduction of 
piece-rate system and all of them are not permanent 
workmen. Departmental notice was issued on the 
workmen before introduction of the piece-rate 
system, which was done with the consent of the 
workmen. The introduction of the piece-rate 
system by the Company has been a lawful act and 
the Union's prayer for restoration of the old system 
of time-rate with compensation for the loss of 
carnings should be rejected. 


The preliminary objection that was raised cn 
behalf: of ‘the Company is that the Tribunal has no 
jurisdiction to adjudicate on the issue under 
reference, because the issue is not covered by the 
reference. The learned lawyer for the Company has 
argued that the Tribunal has jurisdiction to adjudi- 
cate upon the subject-matter of the reference only 
and cannot decide any matter outside it. In 
support of the contention, the learned lawyer cof the 
Company has referred me to the ruling reported in: 
A.LR. 1959, SC, page 1191, This ruling lays down 
that it is only the subject-matter of the reference 
with which the industrial tribunal can deal. None of 
the parties have any quarrel with this principle of 
law. It is a settled principle of law that in deter- 
mining the scope and nature of the point :cferred to 
the industrial tribunal, a Court must 1070 10 the 
order of reference itself. In the present case, the 
order of reference is very clear. The 15506 is 
whether the introduction of piece-rate system in the 
Winding Section is justified and what relief, if eny, 
are the workmen entitled to. The Union bas 
prayed for compensation for loss of earnings. In 
my opinion, this prayer is covered by 6116 issue 
under reference. If the Tribunal finds that the 
introduction of piece-rate system in the \vinding 
Section is unjustified and if the Tribunal intends to 
give any relief to the workmen, then of course the 
question of giving compensation ‘or the aileged loss 
of earnings will arise. For this purpose, tlere need 
not be any assumption, correct or incorrect. I 
accordingly hold that the reference is maintainable 
in law and the points agitated by the Union are 
covered by the subject-matter of reference. 

The learned lawyer for the Company has argued 
that no notice as required by section 9 has to be 
given in the present case, because it is not covered 
by Schedule Four of the Industrial Disputes Act. I 
am unable to agree with this contention of the: 
learned lawyer of the Company. Introduction of 
niece-rate system in place of time-rate system con- 
templates a change in the mode of payment. Hence, 
it is covered by item No. 1] of the Fourth Schedule 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. ۱ 


The learned lawyer for the Company has also. 
orgued that no notice under section 9A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act is necessary in the ٤۶٤ 
case, because the change in the present case was 
effected in pursuance of an award by a Tribunal 
constituted under the Industrial Disputes Act. In 
my opinion, there is considerable force in this con- 
tention of the learned lawyer. It will appear from 


issue 

(1) Whether introduction of piece-rate system in 
the Winding Section is justified? ۷۷۸۱٢۰ relief, 

if any, are the workmen entitled to? 

AWARD 

In the written statement filed by the workmen as 
represented by 96141009016 Subdivisional Cotton 
Textile Workers’ Union, it is alleged that Messfs. 
India Jute Mill Co, Ltd. runs a Cotton Mill which 
has different departments including Winding 
Department and the Company has in its employment 
in the Winding Department more,..than 80 work- 
men on permanent basis. The Workmen in the 
Winding Department were appointed on time-rate, 
monthly/fortnightly paid system. With effect trom 
16th May 1965 the Management  capriciously 
changed the basis of payment of waxes of the work- 


men of the Winding Department from time-rate to 


piece-rate. As a result, the workmen suffered loss 
to the tune of Rs. 12 per fortnight per head. This 


change in the manner of payment of-” wages was. 


effected by the Management without giving any 
notice under section 9A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. The workmen carned higher wages in the 
time-rate system. Therefore, they raiscd an indus- 
trial dispute before the Assistant Labour Com- 
missioner, Chandernagore, by its letter, dated 7th 
uly 1965. As conciliation failed, the matter ٤5 

en referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. In 
its written statement, the Union has prayed for a 
declaration that the introduction of piece-rate 
system had not been justified and for directing the 
Management to restore the old system oi ٣٢٢ ٤ 
with full compensation for the loss of earnings 
sustained by the workmen with -etruspective effect 
from 16th May 1965. 

In the written statement filed on behalf cf India 
Jute Mill Co. Ltd., the Company has stated that the 
present reference is not maintainable, as no specific 
relief is sought and referred for adjudication before 
this Tribunal. It has further been alleged sy the 
Company that the Cotton Mill Section of the 
Company had started production in the Winding 
Section from Ist February 1960 and the wkers 
were appointed on time-rate payment basis. The 
workers of the Winding Department ave still reing 
paid fortnightly since 16th May 1965. The 
Company has introduced in a section of the Wind- 
ing Department piece-rate system by replacing tne 
time-rate system, which was in force. The total 
number of workmen who have ‘cen affected by 
this introduction of piece-rate system are cnly 24. 
Cimmco Muller machines introduced by the 
Company in the Winding Department have a higher 
productive capacity and with the expectation of 
better production and for giving incentive, piece-rate 
system was introduced by the Company with ۲ء‎ 
from 16th May 1965. This system was irtroduced 
by the Company after discussion with the concerned 
workmen individually and collectively and after 
issuing a departmental notice. This system was 
introduced with the consent of the workmen con- 
cerned.. The Second Omnibus Cotton Textile 
Tribunal, in its award, dated 10th June 1958, fixed 
both time-rate and piece-rate payments for the 
Winding Department and the Companv has acted 
according to the award of the said ‘Tribunal. The 
Company has further alleged that actually efter the 
introduction of the piece-rate system some cf ‘he 
workers who were working in the Cimmco Muller 
machines in the Winding Section are geeting more 


THE CALCUTTA ۹225٢, EX TRAORDINARY, MAY 27 1967, 1685

On behalf of the Union, compensation for the 
alleged loss of earnings by the introduction of piece- 
rate System in place of the old time-rate system has 
been claimed. 0.۲۷ 2 Shri Prafulla | Kumar 
Banerjee, Chief Welfare Officer, has stated that 
there was shortfall in wages in respect of some 
workers and some are getting more. O.P.W. 1 Shri 
Rajat Kumar Das, Winding in-Charge of India Jute 
Mill, Cotton Section, has stated that the Company 
had paid the difference by way of compensation and 
encouragement to work. It is, therefore, admitted 
that there was shortfall of earning of some of the 
workmen after the introduction of the piece-rate 
system. It is admitted that average compensation 
for the loss of earning has been given. Ext. 0 will 
show that average difference between the 08510 
wages of the time-rate and piece-rate system had 
been paid to the individual workmen. From the 
evidence of the two workmen examined before me, 
I could not ascertain if they actually sustained eny 
loss by the introduction of the piece-rate system. 
P.W. ۰۱ Shri Soumindra Rakshit who is working in 
the Weaving Department of the India Jute Mill, 
has stated that his average daily earning was 
Rs. 3.77 before the piece-rate system was intro- 
duced and that his wages became less atter the 
introduction of the piece-rate systein. But in cross- 
examination, he has stated that in the piece-rate 
System he was getting less to the tune of Rs. 4, or 
Rs. 5 or Rs. 6 every fortnight. In the same breath, 
he admits that in the first fortnight between May 
16 and May 30 he earned 26 paise more and that in 
the next fortnight he got Rs. 1.77 more according 
to the piece-rate system. He has admitted that 
Sometimes he gets more and sometimes he gets less 
after the introduction of the piece-rate. He has 
also stated that so far as he was concerned, he got 
more wages according to the piece-rate than what 
he used to get according to the time-rate. He has, 
therefore, no grievance whatsoever. P.W. 3 Rakhal 
Chandra Deb Nath, who is working in the Winding 
Department, has stated in his cross-examination 
that’ he used to take the entire wages and the differ- 
ence on giving thumb impression and that he never 
got anything in excess of what he used to get 
according to the time-rate. But he never says that 
his wages became so much less after the introduc- 
tion of the piece-rate system and has nt teen 2915 
to give any specific figure. It is of course true that 
some workers got more wages sometimes and some 
workers got less wages after the introduction (٤٦ the 
piece-rate system. It is in evidence that the 
Company paid the difference in the loss of earnings. 
It is also not possible on the evidence adduced in 
this case to fix any guaranteed minimum basic wage 
for piece-rated workers. As the average difference 
has already been paid by the Company, the claim 
of the Union for full compensation for loss of 
earning is not Sustainable and_ is rejected. The 
ক are, therefore, not entitled to any further 
relief. 

This is my award.

Ext. F that in the award passed by the First 
Industrial Tribunal in the Cotton Textile Incustry 
fn West Bengal between the employers of 47 Cotton 
Mills and their workmen represented by various 
Union, that the learned Tribunal allowed the intro- 
duction of piece-rate system, as it was beneficial to 
the employer and as it would ensure higher produc- 
tion and lesser necessity of Supervision und as the 
system was beneficial to the worker also. Under 
issue No. 3 of that omnibus award, the learned 
Tribunal held that the system was beneficial both 
to the cmployer and to the worker. It was bene- 
ficial to the worker, because this system is an 
incentive to work and provides opportunities of 
earning higher and higher wages. The learned 
Tribunal allowed the plea of the Bengal Millowners’ 
Association that the very idea of the piece-rate 
system was to give an incentive to work. The 
learned Tribunal held that there was no scheme of 
guaranteed minimum of basic wages for picce-rated 
workers in the Cotton Textile Industry in Bombay, 
Madras or U.P. or in the Jute Textile Industry in 
West Bengal. The learned Tribunal rejected the 
claims of some of the Unions in that omnibus 
award for a guaranteed minimum basic wage for 
piece-rated workers. Ext. F, therefore, clearly 
shows that the change from time-rate to piece-rate 
‘was effected in pursuance of an award of the First 
“Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, passed on 10th 
June 1958. No notice ynder section 9A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act is, therefore, necessary to be 
given in the present case to the workmen concerned. 
In fact, it is admitted by the Chief Welfare Officer 
of India Jute Mill Co., O.P.W. 2, tiat no notice was 
given under section 9A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act when piece-rate was introduced. O.P.W. 2 has 
of course stated that they gave a departmental 
notice and informed the workers piior to that. He 


has further stated that he had called the workers — 
to his office and talked to them in the presence ০01. 


the Department in-charge. This Department in- 
charge has not been examined. Furthermore, there 
is no evidence except the words of mouth of 
O.P.W. 2 himself to show that any devartmental 
notice was given or that the workmen were informed 
prior to the introduction of the plece-rate system. 
The workers, viz., P.W. 1 and P.W. 3, have denied 
having seen any notice. They have also denied 
that they were informed prior to the introduction 
of the piece-rate system. The departmental notice, 
Ext. A, produced before me by the Company, does 
not show that it was really served and was shown 
to the workmen. I must, therefore, hold that no 
departmental notice was given by the Company 
before the introduction of the piece-rate system. 
But no notice under section 9A is required to be 
given in the present caSe, as the change was effected 
in pursuance of an award. 


The Company introduced piece-rate svstem on 
the idea that it would give an incentive to work 
and the carning' of the workmen would Fe higher 
and higher. This matter was also discussed before 
the learned First Industrial Tribunal in the Omnibus 
Cotton Textile case and the Icarned Tribunal 
approved of the introduction of the piece-rate 
system in his award, dated 10th June 1958. I hold 
that introduction of piece-rate system in the 
Winding Section is justified.

ulder this Order in respect of such areas as may be specified in 
the notification ;

OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF POLICE, 
CALCUTTA 


ORDER 


The 28th May 1967 


Whereas rioting, affrays and other disturbances of 
the public tranquillity had taken place recently in 
the different areas of the suburbs of Calcutta as 
defined by a notification under section I of the 
পা Suburban Police Act, 1866 (Bengal Act II 
of 1866); | 


And whereas there is still apprehension of 
recurrence of such rioting, affrays and other distur- 
bances of the public tranquillity within the areas of 
the police-stations in the schedule hereto (herein- 
after referred to as the said areas); 


And whereas, I, P. K. Sen, Commissioner of Police, 
Calcutta, being a Magistrate of the First Class, have 
been specially empowcred by the State Government 
under notification No. 181-G.A., dated the 14th 
January 1964. to act under section 144 of the Code 
of Criminal] Procedure, 1898 (Act ۷ of 1898); 


And whereas, in my opinion, there is sufficient 
ground for proceeding under the said section for the 
immediate prevention of disturbances of the public 
tranquillity and of riots and of affrays within the 
said areas and that in order to minimise the 
possibility of further breaches of peace it is 
necessary to impose curfew; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (I) of section 144 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), read with 
sub-section (3) of the said section, I, the said P. K 
Sen, Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, do hereby

Seas. ae 6S 


.Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, do hereby prohibit 


from the 28th day of May 1967 until further orders, 
any assembly of five or more persons or any 
procession within the said areas, or the carrying of 
any lathis or other dangerous weapons or the doin 

of any act which is likely to cause a disturbance o 

the public tranquillity or a riot or an affray within 
the said areas. |

The areas within the jurisdictions of Entally,

suburbs of Calcutta.

the Calcutta Suburban Police Act, 1866 (Bengal Act

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF FOOD AND SUPPLIES 


ORDER 


No. 3829-FS/ FS /14R-107/67.—30th May 1967.—Whereas the Governor 
is of opinion that for maintaining supplies of rice and paddy and for securing 
their equitable distribution and availability at fair price in West Bengul 
it ig necessary to provide for internal procurement eof by or on behalf 
of the State Government; 


And whereas in the opinion of the Governor the methods of operation 
of husking machines will be detrimental to such procurement unless their 
operation 5৪ regulated ; 


Now, therefore, in exercise ef the powers conferred by section 3 of the 
Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1955), read with the Government 
of India, Ministry of Food, Agriculture, Community Development und 
Co-operation (Departmeat of Food), order No, G.S.R. No. 906, dated the 
Sth ae 1966, as subsequently amended, the Goveruor is pleased hereby 
to make, with the oonourrence of the Central Government, the following 
Order, namely :— 


1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(1) This Order may be 


ealled the West Bengal Husking Machines (Restrictions on Operation by 
Night) Order, 1967. 


(2) It extends to the whole of West Benyai. 
(3) It shall come into force at once. 
2. Definitions.—In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires, 


(a) “‘husking machine” means a rice mill coming within the meaning 
of clause (i) of section 3 of the Rice-Milling Industry (Regula- 
tion) Act, 1958 (21 of 1958), and belonging to that category of 
rice mills which do not have arrangements for processing of — 
paddy before milling and for cleaning of rice after milling, and 
Ga owners of kink do not purchase paddy for milling rice or 

٣21 


1675 


6 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, MAY 30, 1967. (Part: 1 


(b) “milling rice’, with ita grammatical variations, means recovering 
rice or any product thereof from paddy with‘ the aid of power; 


(c) ‘‘owner’’, in relation to a husking machine, means the persun 
who, or the authority تر‎ has the ultimate control over the 


affuirs connected with the husking machine, ond where such 
affairs are entrusted to a mannger, such managér shall be deemed 
to be the owner of the busking machine. 


3. Restrictions on operation of husking machines by night.—No owner 
of a husking machine shall ,دہ ارات‎ or allow the carrying on of, the 
u 


operation of milling rice in his husking machine between the hours of 
7 p.m. and 6 a.m, 


4. Effect on the West Bengal Husking Machin®s (Control of Opera. 
tion) Order, 1966.—The provisions of this Urder are in addition to, and not 
iu পা 9 of, the provisions of the West Bengal Husking Machines 
(Control of Operation) Order, 1966. 


5. Powers of entry, search, 861:0۴٥, etc.—(1) The District Magistrate 
or the Deputy Commissioner of a district or any officer not below the runk 
of Sub-Inspector of Food and Supplies in the Department of Food und 
Supplies, ا وو‎ of West Bengal, or any police officer not below the 
ronk of Assistant Sub-Iuspector or any other officer not below the rank of 
Assistant Sub-lnapector of Police duly authorised in this behalf by the 
District Magistrate or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case may be,. may, 
with a view to securing گر اسان‎ with this order or to satisfying himself 
(hat this Order has been complied with :— 


(a) inspect or cause to be inspected any book or document as well as 
any stuck of rice or paddy belonging to or in the custody or 
possession of the owner of a husking machine and take or cause 
to he taken extracts from or copies of, any such book or 
ducument; | 


(৮) require the gwner of a husking machine to give any information 
in his possession with respect to storage of rice or paddy; 


(c) enter, inspect or break open and search, with such aid or 
assistance as may be necessary, any place or premises where the 
. operation of milling rice by a husking machine is carried on; 


(d) seal a husking machine or remove any detachable part thereof if 
he has reason to believe that operation of milling rice is being 
or is about to be carried on in that husking machine in contraven- 
tion of the provisions of this Order; 


(e) Search, seize and remove with such aid or assistance as may be 
necessary, the entire quantity of any stock of rice or paddy alon 
with the packages, coverings ar receptacles in which auch stoc 
ia found if he has reason to suspect that the provisions of this 
Order have been, are being or are about to be contravered in 

respect of auch stock or any part thereof and thereafter take or 

টিপি the taking of all measures necessary for securing the 
production of the stocke of rice or paddy, packages, coverings 
or receptacles so seized either in a court or before the Collector 
of the district under the provisions of sections 6A to 6D of. the 

Essential Commodities Act 197 (10 of 1955), and for their 8816 

custody pending such production. 


2) The provisions of sections 102 and 103 of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1898 (5 of 1898), relating to search and seizure shall, so far as 
may be, apply to searches and seizures under this paragraph. 


-By order of the Governor,
